subsubtopic: IMPORTATION OF AMERICAN BAKERY PRODUCTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The Canadian bakery industry, representing some 30,000 jobs, faces a very real threat due to the rapidly escalating price of Canadian flour in the widening gap between domestic and American flour prices. Because this situation makes it much cheaper to produce baked goods in the United States, and has resulted in more and more baked products being imported from the United States, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin):
That the Minister of Agriculture immediately convene a meeting with representatives of the Canadian bakery industry in order to hear its concerns and consider ways of stemming the importation of American bakery products.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT FOR STATEMENT SIGNED BY NOBEL PRIZE LAUREATES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Yesterday an historic statement of concern on the issues of hunger and underdevelopment, signed by 52 Nobel Laureates, was released simultaneously in Europe and at the United Nations. Among the signers was a distinguished Canadian Nobel Laureate, Dr. Gerhard Herzberg. The statement appealed "to all men and women of good will, to all those in power and to all ordinary people, whatever their responsibilities may be, to bring back to life the millions who, as victims of the political and economic upheavals of the world today, are suffering from hunger and privation". I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That this House draws the attention of all Canadians to an historic statement of concern on the issues of hunger and underdevelopment signed by 52 Nobel Laureates which was released simultaneously in Europe and at the United Nations, and commends the Nobel Laureates for this initiative to aid the plight of 800 million people who live on the margins of society.

subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS TO AVERT STRIKE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgency. It appears that little progress has been made at the bargaining table between the Canadian Union of Postal Workers and the Treasury Board. The government is apparently unwilling to accept many of the recommendations made by the conciliation board chairman, Pierre Jasmin. In light of the fact that the postal union is in a position to go on strike Monday night, and that such a strike would cause severe interruption of a vital service to the Canadian public, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale):
That the government undertake to negotiate in a meaningful way with representatives of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers in an effort to avert such a strike.

That this House calls upon the federal government to launch a judicial inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the licensing, operation, and collapse of Astra Trust and related companies, and in particular to answer the following questions:
(1)	Why was a licence granted when reports were available questioning the bona Tides of the principals of the company?

SUGGESTED STUDY OF URANIUM INDUSTRY-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent importance under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The world will be moving more and more toward nuclear energy use, giving rise to increasing concern and apprehension as to nuclear weaponry proliferation. Canada is and will be playing an ever-increasing role in the supply of uranium fuel and safeguarding against the inappropriate use of such fuel. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bruce Grey (Mr. Gurbin):
That the government undertake a uranium inquiry by reviving the 1980 resolution of the Progressive Conservative government establishing a joint committee of the House and the Senate to examine and report on all aspects of Canadian uranium mining, processing, use and marketing, both domestically and internationally.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
Before I recognize the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) on orders of the day, I would
House of Commons
like to say to the House that today marks the thirtieth anniversary here of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris as a representative of his constituency. His representation is continuous, without a break, and he has justifiably earned the title Dean of the House of Commons.
Editor's Note: At this point the hon. member for Brandon-Souris was accorded a standing ovation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: Since the return of the writ on July 16, 1951, the result of a byelection held June 25, 1951, as members know, the hon. member has had a very distinguished career. He has served as an alderman for the city of Brandon, as mayor, as a member of the legislative assembly, as a member of this House, and as a minister of the Crown. Also he has had a very distinguished career in the Royal Canadian Air Force during which time he was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross. I now give him the floor.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I hope I have your permission to make a preliminary statement and then ask my questions. After 30 years I suppose a situation like this is best described in the words "I am a survivor". I think it was Premier Khrushchev who was once asked what he did during the Stalin years, and he said, "I survived."

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
We in Canada do not need to have any fears with respect to that kind of survival. However, I would like to make one point. I suppose one should make a profound statement on an occasion like this, and I borrow that French phrase:
plus qa change, plus c'est la meme chose.

The more things change, the more they are the same.
I came to Parliament as a member of the opposition. I am still a member of the opposition.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
I came into Parliament when the late C. D. Howe was the minister of everything, as we used to say back in those days. I suppose, if I may put it into the contemporary context, he would combine in his person our present minister of resources, the Minister of Finance, and even the Prime Minister himself as constituting the whole part and parcel of government, with one exception, and I say this to the Minister of Finance. The catch word in those days was, "What's a million?" Today it is, "What's a billion?"
Money values have changed obviously. It is an honour to have served in this House for a period of 30 years. I have established warm friendships on all sides of the House. This is

June 25, 1981
House of Commons
something that people outside Parliament cannot appreciate when they see the rough and tumble of debate. One of my friends recently came to the House during one of the heated moments of debate and said, "Now I understand the meaning of original sin". That is what it might look like to people looking from the sidelines.
I had a very good relationship with the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey), especially when we were both engaged in helping to resolve the postal strike pre-Christmas, back in 1975.1 was in hospital at the time-

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: I almost was.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
-undergoing some heart surgery. There arrived at my hospital room a tape. The hon. gentleman knew I was fond of music. The title was quite significant under the circumstances. It was "The Sound of Music". He might send a copy of the same tape to other people of whom I can think, for "music hath charms to soothe the savage breast". We have had tragedies in our family. But one of the things I remember with great appreciation was the rallying of members of Parliament from all sides of the House. Incidentally, the first letter I received came from the late governor general, Georges Vanier, who had great sensitivity in these matters.
We were stricken with severe disability 15 years ago in the bosom of our family. Today in the Year of Disabled Persons, 1981, it has been my privilege to be involved in a vitally important exercise. I think it is fitting that we are again honouring Terry Fox who, more than anyone, has raised the level of awareness of the special needs and the special abilities of the disabled. It has been my privilege through the parliamentary process to help change what was tragedy into what we believe is going to be a triumph and a major breakthrough on behalf of disabled people in this country.
We have had a parliamentary prayer breakfast, believe it or not, all through the years. Sometimes the public believe that the only kind of praying that parliamentarians do is spelled "preying". The prayer group has been a source of warm fellowship to me over the 30 years.
Finally, I pay tribute to my constituents who, for 30 years, have seen fit to support me during 12 elections. I have had only one slogan: Has served, is serving, and will serve. They have accepted that slogan as a sincere indication of what I planned to do as their representative.
I should point out that my predecessor who sat in this House for a number of years, and also I believe became the Dean of the House, and was a Liberal during all those years, did not get into politics until he was 65. He died in office in 1950 at the age of 81 which precipitated the by-election to which you, Madam Speaker, have referred. He was a very distinguished gentleman. When my Liberal friends ask me if I am thinking of retiring I say, well in light of the experience and the service of my predecessor, I have at least 25 years to go yet!

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: I remember the hon. Bob McGregor who used to be known as "Silent Bob". Some members will remember him. He became the Dean of the House. It does not happen very often, but he had to make his maiden speech in response to what was said by the Speaker in the House. I can remember his maiden speech very, very vividly. It was brief. He said, "If some of you fellows in this House would speak less, you would be here a lot longer." And the next election he was defeated.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. DINSDALE, DEAN OF THE HOUSE, ON THIRTY YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: The verdict was that he had talked himself out of the House of Commons. I am not going to do that, but with your permission, Madam Speaker, I will now pose a question to the President of the Treasury Board, and I think perhaps he knows the subject matter involved.

subsubtopic: ACTION TO PREVENT STRIKE
speechtext: Notwithstanding the revolution in communications technology which is now upon us, postal service is still an essential service in Canada, particularly to pensioners, low-income groups, and small businesses which cannot afford the higher costs of electronic communications and courier service. Arising out of the critical stage of current contract negotiations with CUPW I would ask whether the President of the Treasury Board can assure the House that he has taken the necessary steps to ensure that there will be no interruption in postal services at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: ACTION TO PREVENT STRIKE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is indeed an honour to have the first question from the Dean of the House, and I might say that I am sure all of us enjoyed his remarks. With respect to the question he has posed, clearly in the event of a strike there is bound to be disruption of postal services, but I can assure the hon. member that steps have been taken to ensure that pension cheques and other security type payments will be delivered and that the people of this country, dependent upon that aspect of the service, will be protected.

Madam Speaker, Canada is on the eve of the establishment of a postal corporation. This policy has been in contemplation since as far back as 1962 when it was first recommended by the Glassco commission report. In light of this very significant development which is supposed to represent a major breakthrough in solving the
June 25, 1981

on-going labour problems in the Post Office, and because the public is already in a state of panic over the threatened strike, will the President of the Privy Council indicate what plans he has to ensure to the people of Canada that the mails will go through, and also to ensure a happy transition toward a Crown corporation? I think it would be most unfortunate at this time it we had a breakdown in postal services.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the question was addressed to me as President of the Treasury Board. I remain very optimistic, and I would like to assure members of the House that every effort will be made to bring these negotiations to a satisfactory conclusion. The parties are at the table; they were at the table yesterday, they were at the table this morning, and they will be back at the table this afternoon. I maintain every hope that a negotiated settlement will be arrived at.

subtopic: SERVICES OF NEW CROWN CORPORATION PRESIDENT
SERVICES OF NEW CROWN CORPORATION PRESIDENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, does the government have at this stage of the implementation of the Crown corporation, the postal corporation, the services of the highly reputed new chairman of the postal corporation who is skilful in managerial and negotiating procedures? Are his services available to the government at this time?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: SERVICES OF NEW CROWN CORPORATION PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the responsibility for negotiations with CUPW, that particular postal union, will remain with the Treasury Board until such time as the Crown corporation is proclaimed and in existence. Accordingly, we are proceeding in the normal way.
I would like to point out to hon. members that there is the odd celebrated dispute, but 1 believe hon. members will agree that many, many settlements are arrived at without difficulty, and by and large our record in this regard is quite excellent. I have every confidence in the capacity of our negotiators and, as I indicated earlier to the hon. member, I believe this will be brought to a satisfactory conclusion.

Madam Speaker, my question is also to the President of the Treasury Board. The issues involved in the contract bargaining process between the Treasury Board and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers include proposals for 12 statutory holidays, improvements in premium pay for evening and night shifts, stronger health and safety provisions, and four weeks' vacation pay after five years. In light of the fact that the conciliation board recommended adoption of these proposals, could the minister outline the position of the government on these issues and why there is reluctance on the part of the government to accept the recommendations?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first I point out that the recommendations to which the hon. member makes reference are those of the chairman of the conciliation board. As hon. members know, it was not a unanimous report. As far as individual items are concerned, I think it is best that these be left to the negotiators at the negotiation table.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. If the government is not about to negotiate in a meaningful way with the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, a strike seems almost certain. A postal strike is perhaps the last thing this country needs right now. With the economy of the country in such disarray and the financial burden on almost every segment of the population increasing daily-I am sure the minsiter will agree with that-can the minister tell this House how the government can justify its reluctance to accept the recommendations of the conciliation board when a postal strike would impose severe hardship on the needy, old age pensioners, and small businessmen who cannot afford couriers at $6 a letter and up, and on the millions of other Canadians who rely on the postal service for personal and business transactions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am sure we all share the concerns expressed by the hon. member, but we do indeed have a responsibility to the people of Canada as taxpayers. Surely the hon. member is not suggesting, on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party, that settlements should be made with public service unions in general, at any cost, in order to avoid the inconvenience which strikes sometimes entail.
I didn't say that.

I inferred that from the hon. gentleman's remarks.
However, I would say that these matters have all been taken into consideration. Negotiations are proceeding. I have indicated that mechanisms are in place to ensure the delivery of old age pension cheques and so forth and, as 1 said, I have every confidence that a negotiated settlement will be reached.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before I direct my questions to the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Transport I want to say that I and my colleagues in this caucus join with Your Honour and the President of the Treasury Board in congratulating the hon. member for Brandon-Souris on his length of service in this chamber. We look

June 25, 1981
Oral Questions
forward to being with him in this chamber for many more years.
I should also say that this is the thirteenth anniversary for the class of 1968.

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Of the some 96 members elected then for the first time, there are 15 to 20 survivors. Some of the recidivists include the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody, the Solicitor General, and one or two others.

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. We are into a summer of discontent and dispute between several unions and their employers on the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence Seaway, which could result in severe damage to the Canadian economy. Would the minister tell the House what measures he is taking to resolve these disputes and to prevent a shutdown of the shipping industry? A major part of the dispute is about safety conditions, all of which could be resolved by the government. Would the minister agree that workers should not have to bargain for safety standards and that the government should take these items off the bargaining table and put those standards in place?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: POSSIBLE DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member and the class of '68.
The hon. member's question was quite comprehensive. At the present time there are three collective bargaining renewals-which are at various stages of conciliation-which affect the movement of grain and other goods on the Great Lakes. In two instances conciliation commissioners have been appointed, and in relation to the third one, which involves the Canadian Lake Carriers Association and the Seafarers International Union, I am considering at the present time the possible appointment, as a next step in the conciliation process, of a conciliation commissioner.
The question of what may be bargained is not as simple as outlined by the hon. member, because it is quite obvious that one party to a collective agreement may feel that the safety standards question has been taken care of but another party may make some demands beyond that. There is no question but that the matter of safety conditions in the shipping industry is one which is subject to re-examination at the present time with reference not only to the exact articles but also in relation to where the jurisdiction will lie for the health and safety of workers. However, I believe the essence of the negotiations respecting these contracts involves matters other than those referred to by the hon. member.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CANADA LABOUR CODE TO COVER MARINE WORKERS
EXTENSION OF CANADA LABOUR CODE TO COVER MARINE WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister may feel that one side thinks safety is adequate, but
the other side does not. I remind him that eleven seafarers have lost their lives since the last contract. At least three, and possibly eight, would be alive today had the union's safety proposals been in effect. As I have said before, the government could solve all eight safety problems. Would the Minister of Labour solve four of those under his jurisdiction by extending the safety protection of the Canada Labour Code to these workers? Would he tell us why marine workers should be left to sink or swim and be denied the same protection being given to other workers under federal jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
subtopic: EXTENSION OF CANADA LABOUR CODE TO COVER MARINE WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member will be aware that in the various federal departments there have been, for many years, some 16 different statutes which deal with health and safety in the workplace with reference to different types of undertakings in the country. That is quite aside from the question of employment which falls under provincial jurisdiction.
In relation to the shipping industry, because of the fact that at the time of its passage the federal labour code was made subject to the provisions of other existing federal statutes with respect to safety conditions, that means that the CTC and the Department of Transport still are major factors in relation to safety and health conditions on the ships themselves. This is a matter which is under review and a matter on which there would have to be a governmental, rather than a departmental, decision.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CANADA LABOUR CODE TO COVER MARINE WORKERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, this is a running away from the issue if I ever heard it.

Madam Speaker, may I turn to the Minister of Transport and direct a supplementary question to him, because he could resolve the other four safety issues in dispute between the Seafarers Union and the ship owners. The seamen want water walls as a place of refuge from fire. That is not unreasonable. They want survival suits made mandatory. They want the companies to provide bilingual safety information.
Will the minister issue regulations, which he has the authority to do, to cover these items, and will he enforce the Canada Shipping Act? Will he also assure this House that his department will not put up any roadblocks to prevent the Minister of Labour from extending the safety protection of the Canada Labour Code to marine workers?
Madam Speaker, it is obvious that my colleague was very careful in answering the questions, and I intend to do the same.
Why?

Why? Because negotiations are under way, and they have reached a very delicate point. However, one thing seems sure to me, and I would like to try to make it clear, that it might be unwise to conduct discussions on regulations for
June 25, 1981

safety in general at the same time as negotiations on a labour agreement. That would be very unwise.
I just want to say that during these negotiations I made sure the marine administrator of my department was providing information to both sides as to the progress being made on the three or four points mentioned by the hon. member. For example, there has been progress on survival suits. Standards have been developed by the department. There is a manufacturer offering them now. Progress has been made, and that progress has been communicated to both sides.

subsubtopic: RCMP INVESTIGATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS
speechtext:

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration but in his absence I would put it to the Deputy Prime Minister. subsubtopic: COST OF MOVING "E" DIVISION FROM VICTORIA TO VANCOUVER

subsubtopic: LEGAL AID TO PRESENT AND FORMER MEMBERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Solicitor General. It relates to the charges against certain members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police arising out of the proceedings of the Keable Commission. The minister is reported to have said in the Citizen of June 15, 1981, that:
-his department is prepared to provide legal assistance to those charged, in line with a long-established practice in such cases.
That refers to legal assistance to members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who may be charged.
I want to ask the minister how far does that extend. Does it extend to former members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who are no longer members? Will it extend, as well, to former members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who may have been discharged, but who, during the course of their employment with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, were
Oral Questions
involved in matters which have led to charges or may lead to charges against them?

subsubtopic: LEGAL AID TO PRESENT AND FORMER MEMBERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question relates to an internal policy of the RCMP which provides, in general, that members may be granted legal counsel at public expense if they are charged with the commission of offences in the course of their duties. The very specific questions which have been asked are not necessarily covered by the detail of the policy as I have stated it. Obviously some of the situations which the hon. member may be contemplating will require a specific decision to be made within the force.
To trigger this mechanism, a member of the force makes a request to the commissioner. No requests, of which I am aware, have been made, as yet, in connection with the Keable matters. We want to be fair, and I will be expecting to review the decisions that the commissioner makes in this regard as requests come along to see whether the policy which is now in effect is, indeed, adequate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
It was a question of the adequacy that led to my question in the House. The minister, as a minister of the Crown, reports to the House for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and speaks for the government with respect to them and the policy which ought to relate to them.
Would the minister assure the House that he will advise those who are in charge of establishing the internal policy in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that it is the wish of the government that all members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, including members who were discharged but were involved in matters which have arisen in the course of their duty and have resulted in charges as a result of the Keable Inquiry will, in fact, be covered by that policy, and that, indeed, that is the position that the Government of Canada is taking? I was asking the Solicitor General that question in his capacity as a minister of the Crown.

Madam Speaker, I am not prepared to say that yet. I feel that the decision should be made on a case by case basis, and not in the blanket way which the hon. member suggests. Each member or former member of the force is free to make an application to the commissioner. I have stated the policy. I am prepared to make public the policy statement in its present form. I think that as each case is reviewed by the commissioner, I will watch, and I know other hon. members will watch with interest to ensure that the government does do the right thing by members and former members of the force.

subtopic: COMPENSATION TO FARMERS FOR EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA-EXCLUSION OF OIL SEED PRODUCERS

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture and deals with the compensation payments arising out of the Soviet embargo, particularly as it relates to the payment, or non-payment, for compensation as a result of losses which occurred in the oil seed sector. Could the minister explain to the House and to the oil seed producers of Canada why oil seeds were not included as being eligible for compensation payments under the Soviet embargo compensation payment program?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: COMPENSATION TO FARMERS FOR EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA-EXCLUSION OF OIL SEED PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, to give the hon. member a detailed answer may take longer than necessary. The working model which we use is one of the best in the world. We even had our people go down to the United States to study it. Their people came to Ottawa to show our officials how this model worked, using all price changes and everything that may effect the price of the commodity. Under some of the most capable people in the
departments concerned, led by Dr. Stu Borland from my department, we did everything we could to try to make a payment available to them. Actually, the prices showed an increase at that time and a larger amount of sales to the U.S.S.R. than at normal market time.

subtopic: FACTORS INVOLVED IN DECIDING AMOUNT OF COMPENSATION
FACTORS INVOLVED IN DECIDING AMOUNT OF COMPENSATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister should know, first of all, that there is a direct relationship between feed grains and oil seeds because both are used for animal feeds. The minister should also know that, according to the government policy statement, payments were made not on the loss of sales but on the price of these commodities, and the price of rapeseed, canola-seed, had dropped very dramatically during that period. Given those factors, surely the minister cannot stand in his place and rely upon the Americans to make that value judgment. Surely that decision could be made right here in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: FACTORS INVOLVED IN DECIDING AMOUNT OF COMPENSATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Americans did not make any judgment whatsoever. We just used the working model. We used the system that they used which is considered to be the best in the world. It was developed in the state of Missouri. If the hon. member would like, we can make arrangements for members to have Dr. Borland's group present the facts the way they were presented to us, showing how they studied the markets at that time-all aspects of markets, everything that had an effect on it. There is nothing that the Minister of Agriculture would like to be able to do more than hand out some more money to farmers, but there is no way that I could do it from that fund.

speechtext: Would the House give me permission to make a ruling although the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) is not here? Is that agreeable to the opposition House leader?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-PROPRIETY OF SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A)- RULING BY MADAM SPEAKER
speechtext:
I want to rule on the matter raised by the hon. member for Calgary Centre about Supplementary Estimates (A) 1981-1982, which were tabled on June 3 last. These estimates contain but one item, vote 20a, Energy, Mines and Resources.
What is interesting is that the hon. member in his intervention does not complain about that item, and probably with good reason because that item, vote 20a, fulfils to the letter the requirement of an estimate or vote; that is to say, it seeks approval to spend, and cites the legislative authority on which the request is based. Rather the hon. member's point of order relates to, and I believe for the first time, the description or information concerning a statutory item that accompanies Vote 20a in these Supplementary Estimates (A).
The hon. member objects that it is not in order for the estimates to contain information on government revenues because they should relate only to expenditures. As a second reason he says, in effect, that the statutory item is irrelevant to the item to be voted and therefore, while it is not only improper to show any offsetting revenue, it is aggravated because the revenue shown has no relation to the expenditure. Finally, he alleges that the statutory item anticipates legislation that will establish a fund at some time in the future and at this moment in time has no basis in law.
In reply, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) agrees that the fund in question is yet to be established but adds that this netting or offsetting of revenue shown will not occur until that fund is supported by legislation. For the moment its purpose is simply to convey information.
While the arguments here are very technical, the real issue is the question of the form in which the government prepares the Blue Book of Estimates for submission and tabling in the House of Commons. Members will appreciate that the form of the Estimates has been the subject of debate for many years and I expect that will continue. As I understand it, changes have been taking place over the years as a result of recommendations from many quarters, including the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. But this is an ongoing matter of public debate and not for the Chair to decide.
Therefore, while the hon. member has submitted very interesting arguments, and while the Chair will continue to rule on the propriety of votable items, I must rule that the matter raised by the hon. member does not constitute a valid point of order.

1978-	11.4 per cent

1981-	(2 months)-20.2 per cent.

The 1979 statistics for motor vehicle manufacturers, show that 39,008 person-years were used in the production (assembly) of 1,586,238 vehicles, of which 960,614 were automobiles, 615,326 were trucks and 10,298 were buses. The employment figures cannot be allocated by type of vehicle.
Based on these data, the average number of person-years used in the production (assembly) or 1,000 vehicles was 24.6, in 1979. Productivity in the automotive industry does vary considerably by volume of production run and is therefore significantly influenced by the size and type of automobile.
In addition to employment in the actual production (assembly) of vehicles, there is significant employment associated with the manufacture of automotive parts and components as well as with the manufacture of products such as steel, aluminum, glass, rubber, plastics, etc., which go into the components themselves.
The total impact on the suppliers industries including parts manufacturers, material suppliers, etc. brings the total person-years to about a maximum of 150.

that the bill be read the third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on previous occasions when speaking to this bill before the House I indicated that, in view of its long history before the House, the bill was one of a housekeeping nature rather than one of substance. In fact, the legislation really conforms with the physical facts that pertain and are in existence. In other words, those head offices-for example, the Economic Council of Canada, Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Canadian Transport Commission and the Public Archives-which were transferred to Vanier and Hull in recent years are not now in accordance with the technical legislation giving them their jurisdiction in the first place. Accordingly, the bill moves to put the legislation in accord with the actual physical location of these boards and commissions.
In addition to that, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Pension Commission and the Pension Review Board are operating in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, and that is not
June 25, 1981

in accord with the technical introductory provisions of the legislation giving rise to the jurisdiction exercised by those agencies.
I took the position that this bill was housekeeping. In fact, the legislation has been before the House, not only as legislation emanating from this government, but it was introduced by the former Conservative government through Bill C-22.
To refresh hon. members' recollection of the bill, I want to say a few words about it. The bill affects those departments or agencies which are subject by statutory requirements to having their head offices and to performing in the city of Ottawa. As I have indicated, the majority of these bodies have been moved to Vanier and Hull with the exception of the one to Prince Edward Island.
In the case of the Department of Veterans Affairs, instead of reading "rather than the head office shall be the national capital region", which would embrace the first commissions I mentioned, the amendment shall read: "or whatever place designated by the Governor in Council".
While the present bill is identical to Bill C-22, it differs from the previous bill C-23 in that all reference to the Farm Credit Corporation has been deleted. This change was introduced following the last government's decision in July 1979 not to relocate the Farm Credit Corporation to Camrose, Alberta. It was judged appropriate, therefore, to delete reference to that move in the present bill. If you do not think this is technical, I do not know what is. The bill is very short and plain. It is a housekeeping matter. This is the position the government has taken all along. With that, I rest the explanation of the legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: RELOCATION OF GOVERNMENT AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not our intention to carry on debate on a bill which the minister described as housekeeping. But in terms of the issues involved, under which the act occurred, this is the act to develop "Fort Fullerton" in Hull. As you know, Mr. Speaker, being the member for Ottawa West, there were great difficulties with regard to the development of the city of Hull, a move that was and still is in some quarters regarded as a surreptitious move of departments across the river. They are there. The buildings are there. When I park my car in the morning, I see those buildings. There is nothing one can do about taking them down brick by brick and moving them back, even if one wanted to. I would not volunteer for the job.
I do not think the bill should be described merely as housekeeping. It is a major piece of legislation in the sense that it involves making legal that which is illegal. It will continue to be illegal until this bill passes here, goes to the Senate and receives royal assent. One wonders what causes of action there might be from the point of view of class actions if people felt like bringing actions with respect to the moving of head offices of government.
The minister was quite right when he said that our government had to look at the facts as they existed when we took
Decentralization
office. We had to look at the realities. I do not know of anything that was handled in a more, to put it at its kindest, unusual way than the development of Hull. It was handled by the previous Liberal government almost without consultation between the Government of Canada and the local municipalities.
When the Portage bridge was to be developed, it was announced by Mr. Fullerton, then chairman of the National Capital Commission. It was going ahead and that was all there was to it. There had not been any consultation with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec or the local municipalities on either side of the river. It was a dreadful mess.
I want to quote what I said on second reading because it is important with the minister being in the House. This is what I said with respect to the relations that ought to exist in the national capital area with local governments. I said at that time, and I quote from page 2525 of Hansard July 2, 1980:
So that members of Parliament will have no doubt about my feelings with respect to the matter, let me say quite frankly that I do not begrudge the good fortune of the city of Hull with regard to this development. However, I say to the House that the government handled it in a very ham-handed, unconsultative way. As a result of how it was handled, a great deal of misunderstanding developed in the national capital area. An opportunity for consultation which should have taken place with the provincial authorities, regional government and others, did not take place until after those moves were made.
I would feel much better if the minister would give an undertaking that this kind of thing will never happen again with respect to his government. I hope it would never happen with respect to any government formed by our party. It did cause difficulties and a great number of misunderstandings. There are still spillovers in the area.
The question comes up about what we should do about it. The buildings are there. In this bill we are looking to make legal what heretofore has been illegal. I am told there is a great deal of goodwill and consultation takes place at the staff level of the National Capital Commission with the local governments on both sides of the river. That is to be applauded.
I have felt for some time that things like this and other surprises can happen if there is not the same degree of consultation at the policy making level of the National Capital Commission. I intend in another session of Parliament to put down a private member's bill that will make room on the board of commissioners of the National Capital Commission for incumbents in the chairmanship of the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton and the Outaouais municipality so that both sides of the river are represented in this federal agency.
I must confess there is one disability with respect to that, and that is that I cannot provide in a private member's bill for any compensation, even for the usual daily expenses. I hope that when that private member's bill comes forward the government will grab hold of it and make it part of government policy. Is there any good, sound reason why, in an area such as Ottawa-Hull, the major landowner and therefore the major mover and shaker of events, the National Capital Commission, ought not to have represented on it representatives of the

June 25, 1981
Decentralization
provincial governments which constitutionally have jurisdiction over property and civil rights, zoning and land use?
In the Outaouais region and the Ottawa-Carleton region, the planning process has been moved more and more away from the provincial governments and into those two regional municipalities. If the right hand is to know what the left hand is doing and if we are to have agreement and consensus with regard to how this area will be developed in the future, it is not unreasonable to suggest that all of the players should be at the table and understand one another.
The reason I would like the government to adopt this suggestion is that it can provide for the normal day-to-day expenses of a commissioner in the person of the chairman of each of those municipalities. I am not suggesting that the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton or the Regional Municipality of Outaouais must appoint that person, but there would be a place at the table for them. I suspect that if that were the case, they would take advantage of it. I can see no reason why they would not do that. I hope the minister will consider that matter even before my bill comes up. I am satisfied that a bill to amend the National Capital Act in that regard would get very swift passage in this House.
Since we are dealing basically with relocations within the National Capital Region, the question comes up as to where the moves should occur. There has been a tremendous concentration in the centre of the city of Ottawa and the centre of the city of Hull, the core of the National Capital Region, by the federal government. In some respects the land use planning of the National Capital Commission and the local governments have collided rather than colluded. That is to be regretted.
I want to call the minister's attention with respect to relocation to the fact that there are official plans of local municipalities within the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton, and I dare say within the Outaouais region, which have within the terms of the planning process provision for the location of government agencies, whether head offices or otherwise. There are some now within the city of Nepean and I know more would be welcomed. The official planning of the city of Kanata with an industrial park, the official planning of the township of Goulbourn, again with provisions for industry, have been designed to welcome that kind of location in those areas. I know the city of Nepean is anxious for a site to accommodate high technology development, and this involves consultation between the two levels of government, the local and the federal governments.
There is an attempt being made to diversify the employment and assessment base within this area. In fact, within the National Capital Region we have the potential for the second growth industry in Canada, energy being the first, the second being high technology. It would be helpful to all those areas in terms of commitment by the Government of Canada to have a demonstrated commitment to the growth of the area as a whole rather than to particular municipalities, not denying them anything to which they are entitled. It is important that
the Government of Canada make some commitment in those areas. I know the electoral district of Ottawa-Carleton, taking in as part, as it does, the township of Gloucester, is suitable and I would hope that the Department of Agriculture might look at sites in the officially planned municipalities of Osgoode. Rideau township now has some with respect to Parks Canada, and there are places for other kinds of agencies of the Government of Canada.
What I am trying to say is that I would like the National Capital Commission, the Government of Canada, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) and others to concentrate their thinking in terms of planning not merely on the core of the National Capital Region, but rather to look out into the regions of the national capital. I can speak, I think, for the municipalities on this side of the Ottawa river, and other members can speak for municipalities on the other side because they know the cases more intimately. This is something I would ask the minister not to lose sight of as he deals with the very important program of planning the national capital, because this bill makes legal something which, when it was brought about, had a great effect, not just in terms of the movement of people but certainly in terms of the development, indeed the well-being, of the central part of the city of Ottawa and Ottawa-Carleton.
It is for that reason that I have joined with the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) and the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) in trying to assist as best I could the Government of Canada in making a decision regarding the Rideau Centre. That kind of development, the convention centre which will follow it and the hotel that will come, can do great things for the central core of this area, and from that pebble being dropped in this lake the ripples of advantage can flow out across the area.
If we are to develop, whether in terms of high technology industry, the tourist industry, or even in terms of other forms of employment for our young people, this will take a great deal of co-ordination by all levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal. This will take a vow by governments, whether formed by the Liberal party or the Progressive Conservative party, that never again will we allow to take place development in the way in which there is no consultation whatsoever, which causes such great upset. That is what we are trying to make legal here by the passage of this bill.
As I said at the outset, it is not our intention to hold up the passage of this bill unnecessarily. I felt I wanted to put that case to the minister, and I intend to keep putting it to this government at every opportunity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words about Bill C-13 before the House today and I shall be brief.
Much of the bill is basically symbolic, although it deals with a number of very important moves made in the past. I want to associate myself at the beginning with the words of the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), who talked about
June 25, 1981

the lack of consultation before the move to Hull. I can remember not only concern by people on the Ottawa side of the river, but a lot of concern by people on the Quebec side. I remember the 1976 election campaign in Quebec, for example, when the move was an issue in the local Hull constituency, and was one of the reasons a lot of the people in that constituency voted against a long time Liberal member and voted for the Parti Quebecois, electing to the National Assembly a friend of mine, Jocelyne Ouellette. One of the issues was the relocation of federal buildings without adequate consultation with the government of Quebec, which by the way was the government of Mr. Bourassa in those days, and the city of Hull. The federal government failed to practice what I call, and perhaps this is a new term, democratic federalism. The very essence of democracy is to involve people and consult them before one makes very important decisions. I hope in the future that kind of consultation will be carried on automatically by the government of this country.
For example, many people in that part of Hull were moved out of their homes very quickly. There was not adequate compensation in many cases. Neighbourhoods were destroyed and people were dispersed throughout the city and throughout the Outaouais. I think that is a very sad reflection on the predecessor of the present minister who now occupies the position.

I am interested in making a few comments on the move of the veterans pension commission to Prince Edward Island and the serious problems that is causing for the department and especially for veterans. This is covered under Part II, which deals with the Pension Act. There is a reference to the Statutes of Canada, P-7, which is a direct reference to veterans affairs and the Canadian Pension Commission. In addition, the Department of Veterans Affairs is very much affected by the Public Archives Act.
Another point the minister did not cover is that if we are going to be moving government departments either across the river or across the country, it causes very serious problems for the departments concerned if staff do not want to move. The matter whether employees have to move if a government department is being moved was raised just a few weeks ago in the Public Accounts Committee. Mr. Brittain, the deputy minister of veterans affairs, gave the following answer to the Public Accounts Committee:
-there is indeed nothing to force a person to stay in his or her job or to resign. There is no job guarantee for the people who choose not to move to the Island. Under the Public Service Employment Act, there is a provision that they be looked at first by other departments who are recruiting. If they have the qualifications to meet the requirements, then they are offered the job. That is the way the Public Service Employment Act and regulations are written. They have no trouble finding jobs.
It is fine that the employee has no trouble finding a job. The trouble in connection with the veterans pension commission is that the chairman of the commission cannot find suitable people as replacements, and he has to hire new people. Many of the new people do not want to move. It now takes up to five years to process veterans' applications. It is all very well for
the government to be moving government departments around, but then heads of departments cannot find suitable people to run the departments. There is no advantage to anyone in a situation like that. We are losing all of the expertise in the Department of Veterans Affairs. The staff do not want to move to Prince Edward Island and we are not getting any clear-cut answers from the Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs as to what he is going to do about it. In the standing committee he always tries to slough it off on his officials. He will not commit himself to anything.
I want to refer to an explanation given by the chairman of the Canadian Pension Commission, Mr. Solomon, at the last meeting of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. He pointed to the problems he is experiencing with the Canadian Pension Commission going to Prince Edward Island. The government will have to consider seriously leaving the Canadian Pension Commission here in Ottawa. Mr. Solomon made a statement to the press today that things will get worse. We cannot accept that things will get worse at the veterans pension commission.
Mr. Solomon pointed out in the committee, and I quote:
-the question that was directed to me really related to the staffing problem and whether we are going to continue to have this problem with respect to the Prince Edward Island move. Certainly, as far as the pension commission is concerned, there is no doubt that we have had a very severe staffing problem. We believe the staffing problem has been caused, in the main, by the fact that members of the staff and, unfortunately, trained members of the staff, do not want to go to Prince Edward Island and have left or are leaving or are planning on leaving.
Where does that leave him? That leaves him holding the bag, and he does not know how to correct the problem.
I am not through with that issue. I was not satisfied with the answer I received from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on Tuesday, so I have written him a rather lengthy letter respecting the serious problems with the move of the Canadian Pension Commission to Prince Edward Island. I hope the Prime Minister will take a serious look at the issues I raised in my letter to him. I will not go into all the details of that here this afternoon; I just wanted to highlight the problems we have with respect to moving government departments.
If we move a government department just across the river to Hull or a little further into Quebec, there are language training problems and problems respecting the language laws of the province of Quebec. Several civil servants who were to be transferred to the province of Quebec have come to me with very serious concerns about whether their children would be able to learn in English. These things have to be taken into consideration.
With respect to the Public Archives, the Canadian Pension Commission requires access to service documents which are held in Ottawa in the personnel records centre of the Public Archives. They are walking over there across the street practically every day, I should imagine, to go through the archives for detailed information on a veteran's background. I do not know what they are going to do if they all move to Prince Edward Island. Somebody mentioned we have great communication today; I do not know whether they are going to be phoning the archives every day to rummage through the files

to find out where some veteran was in 1939 or 1940. The government is certainly going to have to think about that.
They have certainly found a way of streamlining pension applications in the United States, Mr. Speaker. There it takes only 60 to 90 days to process an application, whereas in Canada it takes from one to five years. In fact, we have evidence of some which will take up to six years to process. So I hope the Minister of Public Works will take into consideration the Public Service Employment Act regarding employees who do not have to move if they do not want to. If we are going to have a policy of decentralization and only about 5 or 10 per cent of employees want to move, I do not know how we are going to have room for all the civil servants here when their department goes. I thought these points should be put on the record this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, in regard to these bills. I hope the Prime Minister, the Minister of Public Works or the Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs will come up with some answers in the very near future, especially for the veterans service organizations across Canada who are deeply concerned, and for the many veterans who are dying off before their pension claims can be processed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board) moved
subtopic: SUPERANNUATION AMENDMENT ACT, 1981 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING EARLY RETIREMENT OF AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
that Bill C-65, to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act in respect of the early retirement of air traffic controllers, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure today to propose that the Public Service Superannuation Act be amended to establish special pension arrangements for air traffic controllers. These proposals will introduce, for the first time, pension arrangements which are particular to employees in a specific occupation. The problems of the optimum career pattern for air traffic controllers, their early retirement, and alternative career opportunities have been, as hon. members know, significant issues for many years. The new pension arrangements will facilitate the management of the controller work force and ensure fair treatment for controllers who must be removed from operational service or who have spent many years as operational controllers.
Although controllers' wages and other working conditions already recognize the unique nature of their duties, experience has shown that many operational controllers cannot cope with the demands of operational air traffic control up to the time of normal retirement. Much like professional athletes, air traffic controllers must be in top physical and mental condition. Anything less would compromise air safety and would be clearly unacceptable. At least once a year, air traffic controllers are required to pass complete medical examinations and
demonstrate technical proficiency in order to continue to operate as controllers.

Controllers certainly have shorter careers than other civil servants. A number of countries, including Belgium, France and Switzerland, already offer their controllers special retirement schemes. The Americans introduced in 1972 a complete early retirement plan which we have used as a model. The proposals submitted today are part of a program put together by the Department of Transport with the assistance of the controllers' union, the Canadian Air Traffic Control Association. Their purpose is to help, through an integrated scheme, air traffic controllers to prepare for a second career through retraining or to seek a new position, allowing them to collect the whole or any part of the pension benefits to which they are entitled by way of compensation for their loss of income.
The Department of Transport now provides capability assessment services, vocational guidance and retraining courses to controllers who are retired automatically after at least ten years of operational service. The retraining program has only been available recently. Its effectiveness, therefore, cannot be assessed as yet, but my colleague the Minister of Transport and the controllers themselves appear to be quite satisfied with the early results.

The pension part of the program is contained in Bill C-65, which provides for early retirement for air traffic controllers and, under special circumstances, for the payment of partial pensions while continuing work. The proposed pension arrangements will provide a means whereby controllers can be removed from air traffic control-or can voluntarily remove themselves-without severe economic penalty when the state of their health or technical proficiency might affect their performance and compromise the safe and efficient movement of air traffic. Because the government agreed to the pension proposals in the early part of 1976, the new benefits will be available to any eligible controller who left operational service on or after April 1, 1976. In return for these special pension features, controllers are to make an extra 2 per cent contribution to the pension plan, to be matched by the government as employer.
The proposals in Bill C-65 were included as part of the pension legislation introduced in the House on October 26, 1978. However, as hon. members know, that legislation was only at report stage when Parliament was dissolved on March 26, 1979. The air traffic controller provisions had received general approval at that time, with the exception of deferred indexing of the special benefits and the requirement in certain circumstances for the extra 2 per cent contribution.
[ Translation]
I will deal with indexation in a few minutes, but first I would like to explain the problems created by the additional contributions. During committee hearings on the previous bill on the public service superannuation, the president of the
June 25, 1981

Canadian Air Traffic Controllers Association stated that many members of the association were against paying additional contributions of 2 per cent after the age of 55 and 30 years of pensionable service. According to him, those employees were already entitled to full pension under the existing provisions of the Public Service Superannuation Act and the additional contributions would not translate into more benefits for them. On the other hand, since it is indeed a group plan, it seems contradictory that certain controllers be exempted from paying the additional contributions. Therefore, the government has decided to wait until the new plan has proven itself before making a decision.

The bill now before this House therefore requires that all controllers in operational service make the extra 2 per cent contribution. However, 1 would point out that no retroactive contributions will be required for the period between April 1, 1976, and the date of enactment. The 1978-79 pension bill proposed that controllers make the contribution for the first nine months of the retroactive period. However, for reasons of equity primarily, and administrative difficulties secondarily, it has been decided that the requirement for employee contributions for the first nine months should be waived.
I spoke a few moments ago, Mr. Speaker, about the indexing arrangements in the earlier bill, which had as one of its general proposals that there would not be any cost of living adjustments paid before age 60, except for disabled pensioners and survivors. CATCA, that is, the union, argued strongly and convincingly that there should be immediate cost of living adjustments for air traffic controllers who are removed from their position. The present bill therefore includes such a provision, and is also less restrictive than in the earlier bill for employees who leave of their own accord. I would add, Mr. Speaker, that these indexing arrangements are in line with the original 1976 agreement.
Apart from these two exceptions on contributions and indexing and some technical fine tuning, the bill before us is essentially the same as the proposals presented in 1978. As in 1978, we are proposing that any employee with at least ten years of operational service who is moved from air traffic control be allowed to retire on a reduced pension, or draw a partial pension while remaining employed in some other capacity. Employees required to leave after at least 20 years of operational service would be eligible for a partial pension if they move to another job, or if they retire from the public service altogether for an unreduced immediate pension.
Controllers are required to leave operational work if, for example, they cannot meet the medical requirements of an ATC licence, if they have lost their technical proficiency, or if management is concerned that continued service would seriously jeopardize their physical or emotional well-being. [Translation]
Controllers aged 45 or more who want to retire after at least 20 years of operational service would be entitled to a reduced pension as soon as they resign from the public service. Con-
Early Retirement
trollers aged 50 or more with 25 years of service would be paid full pension. Those who voluntarily leave the service in the operational service would not get any partial pension.

As hon. members know, we are examining a number of the features of the public service pension plans with an eye to possible change. I have already indicated our intention to prorate the first cost of living adjustment for anyone retiring on or after January 1, 1981, and we plan to introduce further amendments at a future date. But the provisions in this bill cover pension arrangements for air traffic controllers only. They are designed to recognize the need for earlier retirement and to preserve the safety and efficiency of the air traffic control system. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member who just sat down knows, there has been a great deal of discussion about this bill and the importance of it to air traffic controllers over the last number of years. If one were to ask an air traffic controller what he thought about this bill in terms of its introduction, he would say that it is long overdue. I do not say that in the sense of any criticism, because I know how these things happen. However, that is what he would say.
I think that all members of the House who look at the bill as described by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) would have to say that it contains a great element of fairness. It recognizes the peculiar nature of the work of air traffic controllers, work which has stresses which few of us could imagine unless we were placed in their shoes, and that is impossible. However, anyone who knows an air traffic controller or a group of them and has spoken to them knows the peculiar strains which their work can have on their health and ability to function. Therefore, somehow or other, the government has had to marry the concept of safety on the one hand, which is important, with the idea of fairness on the other. The third concept is the recognition of the facts as they apply to a particular profession.
We have a special bill. What do we do with that bill? It is possible for us to debate the bill this afternoon and send it to a committee where it can be studied; but I think that would be most unfair. I think it is the kind of bill which should be dealt with here and now, today, in a Committee of the Whole House, and we can do that later on this afternoon. Then it should move immediately into the third reading stage and the bill should move out of this place into the Senate. It is a bill which has been around for a long period of time and I think it serves, quite appropriately, a group which need assistance in a particular way because of the nature of their work.
During the course of his remarks, the minister made a statement with respect to a program within the Department of Transport on the retraining of air traffic controllers, who are people who still want to function within the public service. He indicated as well that it was a matter, the efficacy of which he could not as yet comment on because it was quite new. Speaking for my own party, I hope that a year from now we

Early Retirement
can have a statement from the minister, whether or not it is in the House of Commons, about how that program of retraining is working. There are great changes, and not just this one, having to do with health as it relates to safety in transport. I have spoken in the House of Commons previously about the necessity of training. I hope that while the President of the Treasury Board will be assessing the particular training problems which affect the licensing of air traffic controllers, and the strictness which must be observed so that public safety can be protected in terms of that licensing, he will also not let his attention stray from the importance of developing, within the public service, retraining programs for public servants who find themselves caught in a process of change which seems to be moving rather quickly.
There have been consultations with various associations, I know. The president of CATCA spoke to me the other day and indicated the importance of this bill to the members of his association. I have looked at this problem before, and I can only say "hear, hear" to what he told me on the telephone.
Therefore, I am glad that the bill is brought forward today. I am very pleased to be able to say, on behalf of our party, that in order to speed it through so that it can get through the legislative process as quickly as possible, we are prepared to deal with the bill in Committee of the Whole this afternoon and go on to third reading.

There are more cases of these marriages. I should not call them second marriages and I always write back to these people and tell them the

problem is not because there is a second wife involved, it is that the marriage took place after the man's retirement. A first wife, if married after retirement, would not qualify and a second wife married before retirement would.
The number of people that this affects is increasing, partly because of longevity and partly because of earlier retirement, and I think the problem has to be addressed, Mr. Speaker. I wrote a letter at some length on this subject to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) some time ago because it came up in some House business discussions. He assured me that he would send copies of my letter to the President of the Treasury Board, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne), the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and others who have these plans before them.
I raise this point now to ask the President of the Treasury Board to address himself to the problem in any further reviews of the Public Service Superannuation Act that take place. The problem is already there. I have raised it a good many times. A number of years ago when we were in committee on the Public Service Superannuation Act, I thought we had almost got to the point where we were going to remedy the situation but the government backed off.
As I say, the problem has increased through early retirement and greater longevity and it is an issue that the minister should consider. Perhaps when we are in Committee of the Whole on the bill he might answer this representation on my part even if all he can say is that he will study it a little more than it has been studied in the past. I hope that at least he will do that.
Still complying with my own stricture that we deal only with what is in this bill, I draw attention to the fact that, in referring to Bill C-12 of a couple of years ago, the President of the Treasury Board noted that it contained a provision to adjust the first indexation that takes place in January after a public servant retires in order to put it on a prorata basis. The minister says that the government has already announced that it intends to do that this year, making it effective as of January 1, 1981. 1 was not surprised when I heard that announcement because, as I say, it was part of Bill C-12, which we considered in the Thirtieth Parliament.
1 should like to make this point to the President of the Treasury Board before he pushes that matter too far. Plausible though it may sound to give a public servant who retires in November or December a much smaller increase in January than would be given to the person who had the whole year, that would have been acceptable in the days when inflation was not so severe and when the changes over the last six years of employment were not so great. In other words, when those changes were not so great, and when a public servant retired with, say, 30 years of service, which would give him 60 per cent, it was 60 per cent of the average pay for those last six years, and the average of those last six years was not very much below what he was making at the point of retirement.
At the present time, however, in a public servant's final six years there can be a tremendous increase in his salary over what it was in retirement minus six to what it was at the point
Early Retirement
of retirement. When he is given only 60 per cent for 30 years' service or 70 per cent for 35 years, on the average of those six years he will receive a much greater drop from his pay in the last year he was working to his superannuation than has been the case over the years. I know that public servants who are concerned about this will admit that it sounds plausible to go for this pro rata basis but, say, by retiring in November or December the little bit of bonanza they get in January makes up for the other.
I will tell the President of the Treasury Board that I am not asking for it both ways. I am not asking to change the six-year basis and keep the bonanza. If he cannot change the six-year basis, however, then they have a right to think that the bonanza, as I have called it, is something to which they are entitled.
I would urge that the minister be very careful about removing that right to full indexation in January before he does something about the six-year average. If he will change that, I think it has to come down to two or three years. Then I would say that it would be quite fair that the first indexation would be on a pro rata basis. I hope that the minister will look at that very carefully.
I have been asked a few times why it is that some of us do not ask as many questions about public service superannuation as we used to. I suppose the plain fact of the matter is that we did not want to put ideas in the minister's head to do things to restrict the Public Service Superannuation Act. We still want improvements. We want the two or three-year average. We want the corrections with regard to wives as survivors where a marriage takes place after retirement. We want guarantees about the maintenance of indexation. In fact, I have said many times, and it has been said by Liberals too, that the answer to those who complain about public servants getting indexation is not to cut it back or take it away from them, but to legislate indexation for all pensions plans.
I must not carry on much longer, Mr. Speaker, or you will say that I am violating my own stricture that this is a restricted bill. I leave it at that. We welcome early retirement for air traffic controllers. We think the arrangements set out in the bill are good and fair. They are certainly acceptable to the Canadian Air Traffic Controllers' Association. We are happy to see the bill go through all the way today, but I hope the minister will give consideration to the other points to which I have referred.

Consequently, I am pleased to propose the second reading of Bill C-68, an act to amend the Currency and Exchange Act, first reading having occurred on June 22, 1981. The aim of this bill is to permit the governor in council to issue gold coins. Permission was already granted further to an amendment to this act, approved June 20, 1978, which amendment was limited to January 1, 1981.
The debates of the committee and of the House of Commons before the adoption of Bill C-39, in May, 1978, centred on the opportunity of launching a Canadian gold bullion coin program, as suggested by the Canadian Mining Association and other groups from private industry as well as by the Canadian gold mining industry. These discussions raised considerable interest and a great deal of enthusiasm from both sides of the House, after which the members of the opposition recommended a prompt start to the program.
Following representations by certain members of the opposition, Bill C-39 was modified to limit the legislation's power relative to the issuance of gold coins to January 1, 1981, and also that the minister responsible report to Parliament on the administration of the program during the month of December 1978 and every six months thereafter. The aim was to permit gold coin programs for a three-year trial period, after which we would undertake the evaluation of the results.
Afterwards, the Royal Canadian Mint was authorized by the governor in council to launch a gold bullion coin program and the board of directors of the Mint was commissioned to evaluate the results of the program, to eventually inform cabinet, through myself as minister responsible, of the advantages of such a program to Canada and also of the consequential effects on the Canadian gold mining industry as well as the relevant facts that come into play, such as inflation, the balance of payments, the profitability of such a program and other aspects.
