Consequently, the board of directors of the Mint retained the services of Price Waterhouse Associates to evaluate the gold Maple Leaf program and, in effect, gave them broad terms of reference for their evaluation. The evaluation has been completed and the report submitted to the board of directors of the Mint. The board of directors has approved that recommendation and I can only qualify the recommendation from Price Waterhouse as being completely positive. [Translation]
The report from Price Waterhouse Associates was approved unanimously by the board of directors of the Mint, who then recommended that I seek the necessary authority to continue the gold Maple Leaf program on an ongoing basis. The Royal Canadian Mint has never asked the government for financial assistance to carry out its operations since it became a Crown corporation in 1969. The last report to be tabled in the House after the Currency and Exchange Act was amended in 1968 indicates that for the period from July 1, 1978 to December 31, 1980, the gross receipts from the sale of gold coins amounted to $1,456,911,000, and the net profit to $31,682,500. The gold coin programs have benefited the various private companies involved in the advertising, processing and sale of precious metals, the supply of materials, the provision of transport services and comprehensive insurance. They have benefited as well every government which levies a provincial tax on coins sold in Canada.
Last year, in northern Canada, that is north of the 60th parallel, I had the opportunity to explain to the inhabitants of that area the exceptional benefits of the program now under way, and I am very pleased to see that the hon. member for the Northwest Territories, for the riding of Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), will be here to voice the official opposition's views. I look forward in a very positive frame of mind to hearing his remarks which I trust will be approving. The gold required by the Canadian Mint for making the coins authorized by the government, as a result of the amendment to the Currency and Exchange Act and the 1978 amendments, came from Canadian mines or, whenever there were shortages, from the gold reserve of the foreign currency account of Canada.
The gold Maple Leaf coin, offered for the first time in September of 1979, was very well received throughout the world, as results proved during the first four months of sale in 1979: one million coins were sold. That coin was considered a valuable option for dealers in gold, international bankers and investors who were looking for an alternative to the South African Krugerrand which had been on the market since 1967. The only reservation ever expressed about the Canadian gold leaf coin was that the program was only temporary. Such a reaction influenced the strategy adopted for the marketing and promotion of the coin. Official North American and European distributors were therefore most reluctant to encourage investment in a product whose future was dubious. All those who took part in the gold Maple Leaf program, and more specifically the representatives of the gold mining industry, are very anxiously waiting for a favourable decision on the part of this Parliament, hoping it will agree to extend the gold coin programs.

That is why I am most pleased at the prompt and complete way this chamber has decided to deal with this bill at this time.
The Canadian gold coin program, that is, the $100 gold coin commemorating special events and the $50 gold coin commonly known as the gold Maple Leaf, are prestigious items for Canada and have attracted world wide attention to the importance of the gold mining industry in our country. speakeroldname: Mr. Gerald Laniel (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to continue the remarks I began the last time motion No. 33 was before the House on February 12, 1981. Notwithstanding all the opinions which were expressed in good faith at that time, I think it is my duty to put forward some of the facts and rules laid down in the law which dictate the actions of FIRA, the Foreign Investment Review agency.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, as 1 have just said, I am pursuing the comments I started on February 12. The hon. member for Vau-dreuil (Mr. Herbert) moved that an order of the House do issue for copies of all agreements, correspondence, notes and other communications relating to the requirement by the Foreign Investment Review agency that Tate & Lyle Limited reduce its shareholdings in Redpath Sugar Limited. It is surely not the first time that this motion has been discussed in the House, since the member introduced a similar motion in 1979. On that occasion, the House was told that the Foreign Investment Review agency had been advised by its chief legal adviser that the said documents were deemed to be privileged under section 14 of the Foreign Investment Review Act.
The motion was discussed further on November 22. The member for Vaudreuil again introduced that motion during this session, that is on January 14 last, and I advised him in an answer which 1 gave in the House on behalf of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), minister responsible for the administration of that act, that the agency
Foreign Investment Review Agency
had received a legal opinion once again to the effect that the said documents were privileged.
What the hon. member is again asking is that the government disregard the provisions of an act adopted by Parliament. Section 14 of that act clearly stipulates as follows, and I quote:
Except as provided in this section, all information with respect to a person, business or proposed business obtained by the minister or an officer or employee of Her Majesty in the course of the administration of this act is privileged and no person shall knowingly, except as provided in this act, communicate or allow to be communicated to any person not legally entitled thereto any such information or allow any person not legally entitled thereto to inspect or have access to any such information.
Without such provisions, Mr. Speaker, for all practical purposes the review process prescribed in the act would be well nigh impossible. Let me explain. When filing a notice the investor must describe his intentions and during the meetings which generally follow he reveals, perhaps not details of a confidential nature, but at least all sorts of information concerning his operations. How can anyone expect an investor to disclose to the government, through the agency, every aspect of his situation, his projects and his intentions if that information is not to be held confidential? He has therefore every right to expect that this information will not be released, at least prematurely, to third parties and, in particular, to potential competitors.
Before deciding whether a proposal is likely to be of significant benefit to Canada under the terms of the act, the government must obtain from the investor very precise information on his projects as well as on the parent company on which he depends and, should it be the case, on other corporate branches. It is obvious that in many cases the disclosure of that kind of information might be detrimental to the investor in the conduct of his business. That is why it was absolutely essential to include section 14 in the act, which reads as follows, and I quote:
Any information with respect to a person, business or proposed business obtained by the minister or an officer or employee of Her Majesty in the course of the administration of this act may,
(a)	on request in writing to the agency by or on behalf of the person to which the information relates or by or on behalf of the person or group of persons carrying on or proposing to carry on the business or new business to which the information relates, be communicated to any person or authority named in the request, or
(b)	for any purpose relating to the administration of this act, be communicated to a minister of the Crown in right of any province or to an officer or employee of Her Majesty in right thereof.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the minister cannot disclose confidential information on an investor other than within the scope of the act and, to do so, he must secure the expressed and written authorization of the person from whom the information comes in the first place. On the other hand, it may happen that, over and above that permission, if a company files an application with the review agency and makes certain details public or publicly announces that it has applied to take
10958

June 25, 1981
Foreign Investment Review Agency
over another company, then a certain part of the information is disclosed because it has already been made public.
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member raised the matter in 1979, the agency had asked the company concerned to authorize the disclosure of the information involved but this was not allowed. Such a refusal should not come as a surprise. Those papers include, among other things, very confidential information on the financial situation of Redpath Sugar Limited and of its parent company. If that information was ever supplied to the government, it is precisely because those companies were protected under section 14 of the act. Otherwise, probably it would not have been disclosed . Those companies did not want that information to be made public, and therefore they did not permit the agency to disclose it, which they had a right to do under the Act.
Section 14 provides for access to information which is essential to the assessment of a proposed investment while assuring the investor that the information is obtained under the seal of secrecy. On the other hand, because of that secrecy requirement, the reviewing process appears to be an operation which the government wants to hide from the public. On the contrary, we try to make the implementation of the act better known, better understood. But we are forced to comply with the act as it is now.
If the minister is planning to amend it so that in certain circumstances some information can be made public or made available to some people, under certain requirements, then we shall see. In the meantime, this act is the law of the land and those who have to implement it must comply with it.
This act gives a privileged character to the information provided by an applicant in the reviewing process of his proposed investment. It would simply be illegal and shameful not to abide by section 14. It would be a breach of trust, just as if we publicized information drawn from income tax returns, and submitted it to the government with the understanding that it would be used only for specific and limited purposes and that it would be kept secret. Would the hon. member himself be willing to let information contained in his income tax return and provided under the seal of secrecy be made public in a high-handed way if he had submitted an application for investment? Corporations have the same right to confidentiality as individuals.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vaudreuil is well aware of the laws that govern the business community and of the fact that the disclosure of confidential information concerning the way a corporation operates may have detrimental effects.
I am sure that many businesses operating in Vaudreuil, especially along the Trans-Canada highway, would be reluctant to submit an application for investment, acquisition or some other type of transaction if they thought that the data they are submitting to FIR A could be made known to all
members of this House. How could FIRA be made to operate efficiently if, as a result of a motion such as this one, the government could disclose information provided under the seal of secrecy? Do you know of any investor who would be willing to make his plans, projects, Financial situation, and R & D programs known if there were any risk of having all this information made public because of a motion introduced in this House? Do you know of any corporation who would want to invest in Canada if it thought that any data submitted in support of its application could be disclosed?
Did the hon. member not express some concern that implementation of the law would have a negative effect on the inflow of foreign investment? This would certainly be the case if we were to change the rules of the game so that the information provided by the investors to the agency when making an application could be disclosed. In fact, there are people who maintain that the very existence of a review procedure, the fact that a company has to provide information and meet requirements, does act as a deterrent to foreign investors. These people consider this procedure bad economic management since they believe that we in Canada need all the foreign investors we can get, whatever access they might choose to get into this country. Therefore, if we want to go on promoting investment, the procedure used must reduce significantly the risk that the information which any company wants to keep confidential will be made public.
However, data obtained from many sources belie the contention of the hon. member and of those who believe that the agency discourages investment. Until now, and this is probably due to this same section 14, according to a recent report published in the United States entitled Survey of Current Business, American subsidiaries in Canada were planning on investing over $11 billion in 1981, and this figure is second only to the investment forecasts for the United States as such. The reviewing procedure in its present form does not discourage direct foreign investment. It simply ensures that such investments will bring significant benefits to Canada. I shall come back to this point later on.
However, when one analyses the direct foreign investment figures, it is important to remember that this type of investment represents only a very small portion of foreign investments in Canada. They are greatly exceeded by portfolio investments, which do not come under the Foreign Investment Review Act. Moreover, foreign investment, whether direct or by portfolio, represents a very small part of all capital invested in Canada. Thus, since 1961, direct foreign investment accounts on an average for less than 3 per cent of the total savings used by Canadians or Canadian businesses to finance capital build-up in Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING ISSUANCE OF GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to be able to follow the hon. Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais), who gave an excellent dissertation on the Canadian Maple Leaf coin program. He told us that this has been a very successful program, and I am inclined to believe him. In fact, we have every evidence to suggest that it has been a very successful program. The minister was kind enough to send over to me at short notice, the report that Price Waterhouse had made on this program. Of course I have not been able to read it in detail, but have just glanced over it. It would appear that the conclusion reached by that firm is that the program is operating as it should and there are no major faults with it. As the minister said, we have been successful in taking over about 30 per cent of the market for the Krugerrand-Maple Leaf type of coin.
This program has been in effect for three years, and it has benefited collectors and people who appreciate the Canadian Maple Leaf coin as a work of art. It has entered the speculative market and it has also provided a vehicle for people to maintain a store of value. With ever-increasing inflation under a succession of Liberal governments, it is no longer possible to store value in dollar bills or in bank deposits. Therefore, many people who have looked to the Krugerrand, and then, three years ago, to the Canadian Maple Leaf for this store of value, are not really speculators but they need such a vehicle because they have so little confidence in the Canadian dollar, with good reason.
I would certainly also like to extend my congratulations to the section of the Royal Canadian Mint which deals in numismatics. I have written that word down because it is sometimes hard to pronounce.
Perhaps the Minister of Supply and Services would be kind enough to confer with his colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), because, as I understand it, some of the blanks for proof coins cannot be manufactured in Canada. Most of the gold is Canadian gold, or is said to be Canadian gold; but to obtain the very lustrous and very fine finish on some of the blanks, I understand that this work must be done in the United States. The gold is shipped out of the
June 25, 1981

country for a certain amount of processing and shipped back into Canada. I believe the actual stamping is done over in Hull.
It would appear that large profits have accrued to the Canadian Mint and to the Government of Canada as a result of the Maple Leaf program. Had these profits been made in the private sector, I am sure that our good friends to the left would have had a good deal to say about the matter; but since the profits which have been realized have been helping to defray general levels of taxation in Canada, that meets with everyone's approval. We on this side would certainly like to see the Canadian Maple Leaf program extended. We have certain objections to the bill as it stands before us, but that is not one of them. We want to see this program go ahead. We think it has been of benefit to Canada. We were pleased to be supporters of the project some three or four years ago, when it was first brought to the attention of the government by the Canadian mining industry and by coin dealers in this country. It is one of those areas where something was able to be done, with the support of all parties in the House, and has proven to be successful.
Our concern in this matter relates to the blanket authority which the Minister of Supply and Services is seeking forever and ever. If Your Honour will recall, when the amendments to the Currency and Exchange Act were made approximately three years ago with Bill C-37, it was done with a backdrop of the problems which had been experienced with the issue of Olympic coins. That program did not work out anywhere near as well as it should have, and certainly not as well as the Maple Leaf program has worked out. We have obviously learned from our mistakes. At that time, we on this side of the House had a concern. We did not want to give the government blanket authority forever and ever to issue gold coins in whatever denominations it wanted, or whatever purity, or whatever type or whatever specifications. That is why at that time we put the deadline at January 1, 1981 and I think we would like to keep it to that. It might be argued that the program has proved to be successful or that historically, the issue of coinage has often been a matter of royal prerogative. Apparently that has not necessarily been the case in the past in Canada, although in a lot of jurisdictions the right to issue coinage has remained with the Crown and outside the control of Parliament. In Canada, the practice has been to have a fair amount of parliamentary control over the issue of coinage.
Apart from that particular concern, which I shall return to later, Mr. Speaker, 1 have a similar but slightly different concern with Section 4(2) of the act as it stands at present and as it will become if amended by Bill C-68. It seems that we are specifying something in a schedule to an act of Parliament and then giving authority to the governor in council to change the act by means of an order in council. It would be my contention that if something can be changed by order in council rather than by an act of Parliament, then, in the first place, it should be left to regulations. Regulations can be changed by that mechanism. However, if it is important enough in the first
Currency and Exchange Act
instance to be put in an act of Parliament, then why should we give to the governor in council the authority to change it?
This particular case does not involve anything of great, overriding concern, but there have been cases in the past where Parliament has come a cropper by granting that type of authority. I might cite the Northern Pipelines Act, for instance. Certain conditions were laid down in that act-not in the regulations but in the act-and then the authority was given to the governor in council to change them. We might just as well have left them in the regulations in the first place. All we did was to give ourselves a sense of security that never really existed.
I believe that the minister and the Royal Canadian Mint would like to see the bill passed into law as quickly as possible.
I can understand that all ministers want their bills passed into law as quickly as possible, and always consider that their bill should have the highest priority. However, in this case I can well understand the concern of the gentlemen at the mint. Perhaps the minister has not been as diligent as he should have been about bringing this legislation forward so that we could give it the full examination it should have. Whereas we cannot accept the bill in its present form and would not give unanimous consent for it to be dealt with in committee as it stands, and then give it third reading today, if certain changes were made, then I think that might be possible.
If the government would accept an amendment to limit the time period and instead of substituting the words "from time to time" in Section 4(1) and (2) for "at any time before January 1, 1981", "at any time before January 1, 1985", that would buy an extra four years. It would put a four-year limit on the authority to be granted by Parliament to the Minister of Supply and Services. That approach would certainly meet with my approval.
Perhaps during the time that remains of my speech, some form of arrangement could be made along those lines. I hope it can because we on this side really do not want to jeopardize the Canadian Maple Leaf coin program.
I was looking forward to the opportunity to ask some questions on the Price Waterhouse report in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to which the bill was to have been referred. I had also hoped to have an opportunity to question officials of the Royal Canadian Mint. If that opportunity does not present itself because of an arrangement that may be reached in this House tonight, perhaps it will be possible at a future date. Many of us have a great deal of interest in this subject.
1 represent a gold mining area, Mr. Speaker. I am coming now to the part of my speech that the Minister of Supply and Services warned me not to go on about at length and that is to extol the virtues of the gold mining industry in my constituency. I shall be as brief as possible.
The gold mining industry is of great importance to the Northwest Territories. We produce about 200,000 ounces of gold per year. That brings about $100 million of new wealth into the Canadian economy. We are justifiably proud of that

June 25, 1981
Currency and Exchange Act
and I should like to think that some of our gold goes into the Maple Leaf coins and that a fair number of those coins come back to investors in the Northwest Territories. There is a program of capital expenditure of around $150 million in progress and on schedule, to develop another major Canadian gold mine.
Gold mining is of such importance to the Northwest Territories that on May 1, 1981, native gold was proclaimed the official mineral emblem of the Northwest Territories. If you would permit me, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read that proclamation into the record. It is not very long and reads as follows:
WHEREAS Gold has long played a major role in the development and prosperity of the Northwest Territories;
AND WHEREAS Gold is emblematic of the enduring value of the wealth of the Northwest Territories;
AND WHEREAS Gold is a fitting symbol of the bright prospects and future of the Northwest Territories;
NOW THEREFORE, by virtue of the power vested in me by the Northwest Territories Act of the Parliament of Canada
I hereby order and declare:
That gold be hereafter deemed and recognized to be the Mineral Emblem of the Northwest Territories.
Done at Yellowknife under the Seal of the Northwest Territories, this 1st day of May 1981.
John. H. Parker Commissioner
I just thought that somebody might be interested in that.
A part is played in the gold mining industry of Canada by the mint that many people are not aware of. Most Canadian mine production is refined at the Royal Canadian Mint. I should like to take a few minutes to say something about this as I have never heard it referred to in Parliament.
In particular, I should like to compliment Mr. Roger Parisi-en, the manager of the gold refinery at the Royal Canadian Mint. This is one of the few federal Crown corporations about which I have anything good to say. It never seems to make political headlines and we do not hear very much about it in the press. That indicates the good job the mint is doing. Their charges for refining are quite reasonable. They go out of the way to assist the smaller gold producers and the smaller dealers in scrap gold and scrap jewellery. I think the refiners who work there, and there are several of them, deserve the compliments of this House. I referred to the increasing necessity to refine scrap jewellery at the Mint. That is, of course, having some effect. This particular material is rather hard to deal with. Very often it has a low gold content and many impurities mixed therein. During the chlorination process, an abundance of fumes are given off. If possible, I would like the Minister of Supply and Services to go to the refinery at the Mint where they process some of this low-grade scrap jewellery so that he can see for himself the type of working conditions which the people have to endure while they process this material. Because of the fumes, the atmosphere cannot be that healthy. Much of their equipment is somewhat antiquated
and is not really designed to handle scrap jewellery. Perhaps the minister could keep that in mind.
I do not always agree with the over-all gold policies of the government. One aspect of the government's policies which I find most objectionable is that of selling Canada's gold reserves by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). I have to admit that the proposal to do this was made originally in the 1979 budget. The idea was to sell off about one million ounces of Canadian gold reserves. But amounts considerably in excess of that have been sold to generate money. Maybe because of high gold prices, that policy has realized a fair amount of profit to the Government of Canada. I may be faulted on that statement, but I would not like the Government of Canada to be engaged in speculative activity on the international gold market. The use of Canadian gold reserves from time to time to produce Maple Leaf coins, when the amount of gold coming in through normal commercial channels is not sufficient, might be okay if we can use our reserves to make up a fluctuating supply. But as a general idea, just to sell off reserves is not something we should do, in my opinion. Reserves in the order of 20 million ounces are about right for a country like Canada. If we take a look at European countries, such as France, we see they are very reluctant to let a draw-down occur in their gold reserves. They like to accumulate gold. I do not think that we in Canada should go overboard accumulating gold, but, by the same token, we should not let our reserves draw down too far.
The classic example of draw-downs on stockpiles of that nature happened in the United States under the Nixon administration. It was used as a technique for getting more money without imposing additional taxes. They allowed the sale of much of the GSA stockpile, strategic minerals for which there was a requirement. But that was done to get ready cash. I hope that we in Canada will not be following that procedure.
That is as far as I want to go on this subject. In general, we are in agreement with this act, with the one provision that I have mentioned. We would certainly like the Canadian Maple Leaf project to continue and grow from strength to strength. That being the case, I hope I have allowed sufficient time for some kind of accord to be arranged. I hope that this bill can receive as swift a passage as is possible.

The House resumed, from Tuesday, June 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres, that Bill C-58, to amend the Canada Elections Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday evening when we were discussing Bill C-58 to amend the elections act I was making a few brief remarks. For the information of many members who happen to have city ridings or ridings which are not as large as those some of us represent, I was trying to bring to the attention of the House that those of us who are incumbents in our constituencies have a profile, having served our constituencies for some time, and we can well appreciate that the 47 days compared to the 60 or 59 days would be of considerable advantage, an advantage not enjoyed by those who are seeking election for the first time within a constituency. While that may be desirable to those of us who are incumbents, I suggest the government is shortening the time because it has more incumbent members than my party or the NDP, and therefore this would be an unfair advantage over the two parties which sit opposite the government. It would be an advantage only to the incumbent members.
Canada Elections Act
I have heard members on the government side, specifically the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher), when speaking to this bill, state that there is money to be saved by shortening the time from 59 or 60 days to 47 days. It has been suggested that those of us representing the constituencies would be able under the present act to initiate savings in our areas as well. However, I would draw to the attention of that member that we will still have advertising for the 47 days, and many of us with larger constituencies will find it impossible to complete our campaign in that 47 days.
My own constituency is some 1,800 square miles and the largest centre of population is 6,000 people. That happens to be the Saskatchewan side of the border city of Lloydminster. My constituency flows along the Alberta border along the North and South Saskatchewan Rivers. Coming along the Alberta side, my constituency touches upon three other federal constituencies: the constituency of Vegreville, the constituency of Crowfoot and the constituency of Medicine Hat. My riding follows the North Saskatchewan River all the way around and back up through North Battleford, joining the North Saskatchewan River and back to within 35 miles north of Lloydminster.
When I first started campaigning after being nominated in
1977-	and this is for the information of members who do not have to travel great distances by road-I purchased a car and used it exclusively for political work. I bought that car in April
1978-	I hope the people from the Department of Revenue are listening-and put 54,000 miles on it by the time of the election of May 22, 1979. Even then I did not have enough time to canvass every community in my constituency. It may be an impossible goal for a member to canvass every dwelling in his constituency, but to do so in 60 days is certainly impossible. The people of Canada deserve the opportunity of meeting their prospective member of Parliament. They should not be denied that opportunity by decreasing the time by 13 days.
When considering the other problems associated with the present elections act I find it strange the government feels that by decreasing the election time by 13 days it will in some way solve some of those inadequacies. I find nothing in the decrease by 13 days that will help those who are shut in at election time. I Find nothing in the decrease by 13 days that will help those who feel it is undesirable to vote by proxy but would like to see mobile ballot boxes. This problem is not solved by decreasing the time by 13 days.
Let me draw to the attention of the House some of the problems that will not be solved by the 13-day reduction. The first relates to the provision of a list which is adequately kept up to date, and the second is the differential between the appointment of rural enumerators and urban enumerators used to provide the information for this list.
In regard to the urban enumerators, the party that obtained the greatest number of votes at the previous election would appoint one enumerator, and the party that obtained the second greatest number of votes would appoint the other enumerator in that constituency. However, with regard to

June 25, 1981
Canada Elections Act
rural ridings, I find that under this bill only one enumerator is to be appointed. I do not see how the incumbent member of Parliament can have any influence in the appointment of that enumerator, if that member happens to sit on the opposition side. Although some might say the government is using this as a form of patronage, 1 feel it is just an oversight on the part of the government. The government does not realize it has treated rural constituencies in a manner different from the manner in which it has treated urban constituencies.
Provincial constituencies are much smaller than federal constituencies. A federal election campaign in Canada lasts 59 or 60 days. A provincial election campaign in Newfoundland lasts 21 days; in Alberta, 29 days; in British Columbia, 38 days; in Manitoba, 35 days; in Ontario, 37 days; in Quebec, 32 days; in New Brunswick, 36 days; and in Prince Edward Island, 26 days. My constituency is larger than Prince Edward Island. There are more than 30 provincial members in the province of Prince Edward Island; I am the only member from my constituency; I feel I should have for an election campaign at least double the length of time allowed for a campaign in Prince Edward Island. A provincial campaign in the province of Saskatchewan lasts 28 days. There are approximately four and a half provincial constituencies within my constituency.
I do not suggest that I as one man campaigning or any one person assisted by party workers campaigning in my constituency should have four and a half times the number of days to meet the constituents there, but I suggest that the 60 days provided for should not be changed. Forty-seven days is less than double the amount of time a provincial member covering less than one-quarter of my constituency would have to cover his riding. That is one of the reasons we feel that this bill to shorten the period for election campaigns is not something which we would want to see passed without further study.
The hon. member for Mississauga North went to great pains when he was speaking in this debate to point out that several newspapers of our country have called for shorter election periods. He pointed out that the February 3, 1981 Saskatoon Star-Phoenix said the following:
Even a minimum of 47 days appears to be too long in this age of speed in communication with voters.
The Chronicle-Herald said the following:
The bill should be put through and made ready for the next election, and not allowed to be withdrawn for consideration until another session.
And while the MPs are at it, perhaps they might consider further reducing the time allotted for campaigning.
The hon. member for Mississauga North quoted the Winnipeg Free Press as follows:
This time, Canadians, by accident, had a campaign of more nearly European length with no ill effects.
It is a very debatable point that there are no ill effects, when we consider the outcome of the election. The article continued:
No one could seriously complain that, in the six weeks they gave themselves, the parties did not have an opportunity to get their messages across to the public. Indeed, the job could have been done quite adequately in a couple of weeks less.
The Toronto Star said the following:
Shorter, sharper election campaigns would benefit Canadian democracy by concentrating debate and focusing public attention on the issues and policies involved.
If the basis of this bill's having been brought forward is editorials or statements made by several newspapers in our country advocating a shorter election period, I suggest this government, by following that rule and not following some of the recommendations made in editorials which have been presented in the last six months condemning the government for other actions, is reversing its policy. The government should not justify shortening election campaign periods by 13 days with statements made by newspapers. Its justification should be the will of the people.
Some constituents have complained that election campaigns seem to be unduly long. Some people have been absolutely fed up with listening for 29 days to political advertisements on television, seeing them in the newspapers or hearing them on radio. However, this will not be affected by the change in this act. I think it is therefore an injustice to anyone seeking election to this House of Commons to shorten the time. The constituents I serve feel they are too far removed from their member of Parliament. I am 2,000 miles away. I am here for five days a week and home only for two. My constituents do not have an opportunity to discuss with me the issues they feel are important. By shortening the period of election campaigns I think we cause people to be further removed from their members of Parliament and further removed from the House of Commons. They are further removed from their representatives, and I do not feel that that leads to good democracy. I do not think that further removing constituents from their members of Parliament will add anything to the democratic process.
In my constituency and in others we have the benefit of fairly good main thoroughfares. However, some of us must follow railroad lines, some of them built 70 years ago. Many of the villages in Saskatchewan were established along such railroad lines anywhere from six to 12 miles apart. The rationale was that that was the distance a wagon of grain could be hauled by a good team. However, people still live in those small villages. There may only be 12 or 20 people. In the larger ones there may be 100. In some towns there may be 500 or 600 people. If we travel by road, we have to stop and get out. We have to go into cafes and elevators. We have to knock on a dozen doors per town. We have to have some time.
I think we would all like to find some way of avoiding extending election campaign periods, but when I was a candidate first seeking office I would have felt that by shortening the campaign, a disservice would have been done to me. If my opponent had been an incumbent, I would have been placed at a considerable disadvantage, especially if I were seeking election for the first time. I was fortunate that my constituency was a redistributed constituency. The member who held the majority of it prior to the May, 1979 election chose to run in a different part of the constituency. My opponent was a former member of Parliament who had been defeated in 1974. He was
June 25, 1981

known throughout most of the constituency. My other opponent enjoyed about the same recognition as I. However, if I had been running against an incumbent, I would have had much more difficulty.
As I said at the outset, I campaigned from October of 1977 until May 22, 1979, and I did not cover my constituency. I did not meet every member of the electorate, as I would have loved to do. By shortening the election campaign period, we are denying the electorate the opportunity to meet members, we are denying members the opportunity to meet their constituents and we are placing new office seekers running against incumbents at a disadvantage.
In closing, I would like to say that I cannot possibly speak in favour of this bill and support it when there are so many inadequacies within our election system. The inadequacies of which I speak are greater than and in addition to the difficulty in having to campaign for 60 days.
1 think everyone is aware this bill was originally drafted by our government, and the reason it was drafted then was that we were in a minority position, an election was imminent and we did not have the ability the present government has of waiting three or four years before having to go to the people. Right now, Mr. Speaker, we have three or four years before another election. We are now in the middle of the ten-year census started June 3, which will bring forth more information as to population distribution and redistribution of constituencies, and indeed, Mr. Speaker, as to whether there will be more seats added to this chamber after the census.
I could understand it if the government had brought forward legislation encompassing the whole of the election act so that we might better be able to conduct an election on the basis of the 1981 census. If that were done and the census information were included-although I do find difficulty in accepting the shortening of the campaign period-and if it were coupled with some moves that I felt were of advantage to the people of Canada, I could accept it. However, as I look at the act now and this shortening of the campaign time, I find it is of advantage only to incumbent members, therefore of greater advantage to the government members because they have more incumbents than we do. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would not be able to support this act.
I would also like to say, while we know that in speaking to this bill we are confined to general statements about the reduction of time, Mr. Speaker, there is again the need to establish a permanent voters' list. There is a need for mobile ballot boxes, and a need to ensure that those unable to vote at a particular time are still able to cast their ballot. 1 do not see that in this bill. I do not think it is anyone's intention either on this or on the government side to deny anyone the right to vote, but when we look at this bill and at the things I just mentioned, we do not see them. So what we would like to say, even though some of us are speaking against the bill as it is, is that we would very much welcome the government bringing
Canada Elections Act
about additional changes to the elections act so as to bring democracy closer to the people of Canada.
There is one thing that has always concerned people of urban and rural constituencies, and in looking at this bill I see it has not been changed. People in rural constituencies who are left off the election list can have a neighbour who is on the list vouch for them and affirm on the day of the issuance of the writ that they are residents. The urban voter does not have that right, I do not know why. I do not think it is because the government of the day felt that the people in urban Canada have no neighbours. I am sure they have them, as we do on the farm. So I think in terms of equality that provision should be in the bill.
I would like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me the opportunity to speak on this bill, and let me say again that if this bill had in it more changes to the act than merely the shortening of the campaign period, I could find myself supporting it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to express some very serious concerns, many of them along the same lines as those raised by the previous speaker. As an individual who has been active in the voluntary political process for more years than I care to remember, I find no redeeming social or political value to this bill whatsoever. The bill is described as follows:
The purpose of this Bill is to shorten the period required to hold a general election from approximately sixty days to forty-seven days. The proposed period would apply to both general elections and by-elections and would be obtained by replacing the requirement that preliminary lists of electors be printed and sent to electors with a requirement that preliminary lists be reproduced in reduced numbers by photographic or other means and that a notice of enumeration be sent to electors.
There is nothing in the bill that refers to any meaningful reform in the electoral process along the lines suggested by the previous speaker. I agree with some, disagree with others, but there is no mention of electoral reform here at all.
The major reason for my strong disagreement is that I believe the bill is wrong in principle and worse in practice. Elections and the political process are too important to be left to politicians alone. They are too important to be left to those who hold elective office, to the paid pros in the political business. They are too important to be left to those who benefit directly in the advertising industry, the professional public relations "flacks" and, if I may use the term-and I mean none of these terms in a derogatory sense at all-the few, the regulars, the party hacks-and I use that in the best sense of the term because I have the utmost respect for those people who continually give of themselves on a paid or unpaid basis in a profession or field which is singularly unappreciated, I think, by most Canadians. However, it is too important a business to be left to those who engage in it for reasons of livelihood or merely because they have a great deal of zeal for the game of politics itself. The political process and elections are too important. To me and to many others, it is important to have people involve themselves in political activity who, while they realize and understand that the business of government is important, usually have other things on their mind, such as earning a

June 25, 1981
Canada Elections Act
living, running a home, paying the grocery bill or trying to build their own business, whatever 1001 things ordinary people see as their priorities in day to day living. Politics is not the be-all and end-all for them, but if democracy is to be healthy, it is important they become involved at some point. You need time to generate activity during the course of an election campaign because ordinary Canadians, the average Joe and Jane who are not thinking about it day in and day out, are not really hit by the fact that they have a choice to make and should become involved when an election is called. For those relatively few in this society, and in most societies for that matter, but for those tragically few in Canadian society who take a serious interest in the business of government and in the business of politics on a continuing basis, to go out and find the people to tap whose interest must be shaken and awakened to get them to participate requires some lead time before you get into the active part of a political campaign.
It seems to me it is vital, and to many others with whom I associate, that we provide the lead time required after the calling of an election, especially in rural and widespread urban-rural constituencies. We must provide time for those ordinary Canadians who have an interest, but not an overriding continuous one, in political and public affairs to be located, activated and mobilized in the democratic participatory political process. Apart from any other differences which we might have in our background and ideologies, surely all of us have a commitment to the idea that more ordinary Canadians should be involved in this business.
Another aspect which was touched upon by the gentleman from Saskatchewan who spoke just before me was the fact that most of us realize that it is important to provide more time for personalized contact between those seeking public office and those who provide the support for candidates who succeed. Whether it be the time taken going house to house or farm to farm to visit with different organizations, whether they be unions or chambers of commerce, to provide personal contact which will make the business more relevant and more meaningful allows those people contacted the chance to feel involved. It will give them the feeling that someone out there really does give a damn.
Unfortunately, many of them out there do not think so, incorrectly, I would suggest. I think almost all of us do sincerely care, but there are a great many people out there who do not share that view. In a day and age when more people feel alienated from society in general, and from the political process in particular, I suggest that it would be absolutely wrong to create a bigger gap by allowing less time for that kind of meaningful personal contact between those seeking elected office and those whose responsibility it is to grant the honour and privilege of representation. By shortening the period of election campaigns, we would be allowing less time for individual contact, less time for the kind of effort which can be made at low dollar costs in terms of involving people and getting the message across in a personalized and direct way. I would suspect that not very long afterward the
push would be on to go to greater maximums of political expenditures so that we can make up for the other by again stressing the heavy capitalization of adverstising in the mass media. As was mentioned before, that is the kind of campaigning that I object to.
During the last two campaigns, and I am sure the hon. member was referring to the 1979 and 1980 campaigns, a height was reached in terms of the head bashing commercials which went on. It appeared that no one in the media was saying anything positive at all. Whether by cartoon, by card tricks or by pictures of shell games, however it was carried out, there was a sickening attitude felt by the body politic out there which I feel those who drew up those kinds of schedules really deserved. The fewer people we have personally and directly involved, the more of the same we will have. More emphasis will be placed on that kind of meaningless and hostile type of commercialization. It will not be an informative political campaign as witnessed in the last two election campaigns.
In a 47-day campaign how can you begin to organize in a constituency such as my own? I have 13 municipalities in my riding. The last election was a winter campaign and I hope that we will never get into one of those again. But if we do, how do you go about setting up all-candidate forums in 13 municipalities and a number of other rural communities in a widespread rural-urban constituency?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: It was an accident last time.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Yes, it was, and you were the accident, my friend.
How do you organize in 13 different communities and do the advertising necessary to allow people to come in and participate? What most people did in our area, and what I suspect they do in many other parts of the country, is to conduct an old-style political forum where people can be tested, where a battle, of wits can be witnessed. In these types of forums the candidates can be cross-examined and put through their paces. That is a healthy process and that is how it should be, if politics is to survive as a meaningful way of life on this continent over the next number of years.
The hon. member who spoke before me mentioned newspaper editorials and the fact that almost all of them called for shortened election campaigns. Quite apart from the fact that I feel they are misled, I feel that it is the media which has the most to gain by over-emphasizing paid commercialism in politics. Over the last number of years, we have become aware of the lucrative opportunity associated with election campaigns. Perhaps they rate next to Christmas, Father's Day, Mother's Day and Easter in lucrative opportunity. I see no redeeming social value to the shortening of campaigns, and certainly the enrichment of the media is not a very worthwhile one either.
As far as the mechanics of election campaigns are concerned, I have had enough to do with returning officers and deputy returning officers over the years to realize how difficult it is for them in many circumstances, even with a 60-day campaign, to find enumerators, deputy returning officers, poll
June 25, 1981

clerks and the hundreds of other people who must be drawn away from their jobs or homes to successfully provide manpower for a campaign at its present length. The same people are not always there to be called upon. In many cases we tend to rely on the same people year after year, so when a winter election is called, people who would normally participate just cannot manage. It is then that the returning officers in the constituencies must go out in a mad scramble, utilizing all parties, which is good, just to find people who are available and able to be trained in a short period of time. Quite apart from the printing time, it will be very difficult to find people to train, since a great many returning officers go more than a little grey, even with the 60-day provision.
The final point I would like to raise, which has been made before, has to do with the element of surprise being always in the hands of the government. Those within this country who are continually going forth on the binge of calling for fixed election dates often use it as an argument that too much power is in the hands of the government of the day, enabling it to call an election at any time it chooses. I think there are more advantages to the public weal of the current process than there would be in having fixed election dates, such as the process which exists south of the border. There would then be yearlong election campaigns, rather than 60-day ones, and the government would be largely inoperative.
However, to shorten the 60 day period even further would really stack the deck, not only in favour of the government of the day, but also in favour of all incumbents. While we who are here at this point may feel rather comfortable at the prospect, we may not always be here, and we certainly were not always here.
I suggest that it behooves us to take a look at what is to the benefit of society at large. One can go overboard. The union to which I once belonged went so much overboard in trying to ensure what it perceived to be the democratic process that at one point it printed its ballots in circles so that no one's name would be on top. That was based on the old western, radical, wobbly tradition. Perhaps that was a little excessive, and no one is suggesting that we ought to go to those lengths, but surely it is not too much to suggest that there should be some lead time provided in order that those persons who have been nominated and have full-time occupations, or those who have not yet been nominated, may have sufficient time. It is not always a matter of choice as to whether or not one thought ahead about one's nomination. Even if one has, and one's occupation is such that one must continually apply oneself to it, one is not that free to get out into the community to become known or to be able to compete on anything approaching an equitable basis until the actual election campaign is called, and that in itself involves sacrifices.
Therefore, I would submit that for all of those reasons there is no compelling argument for the shortening of elections. There is a feeling among the public that elections should be shorter. That is agreed. However, the period to which they are
Canada Elections Act
referring is that period which is now restricted, I believe, to approximately 30 days, which is the limited period in which we can now conduct commercial advertising. That is the part that the public finds offensive. If one wants to limit the period that the public finds offensive, let us cut it down by an extra week. Our purpose here is not to subsidize the advertising industry, after all. In any case, none of us seem to use that time all that constructively in terms of putting solid information or options before the Canadian people. The time is used much more on product identification and repetition than on anything of substance or value.
The other point which was mentioned briefly as well was that while the main and only thrust of the bill is, in fact, to shorten election periods, it might have some value if it dealt with some other reforms, or even opened the door by presenting a few. However, it seems overly limited and does not really provide, within its driving thrust, any option to add items which would involve serious electoral reform. As a British Columbian perhaps, because we have had this process in the province for many years, I think that the process of an absentee ballot would be worthwhile. It is subject to much less abuse than the proxy system. It requires much less bureaucracy and finagling than does the proxy system. It can be utilized well, provided that there is a period of some one to two weeks in a country of our size. Of course, it would have to be a little longer than the one week provided within the jurisdiction of a single province to allow for a delayed count for those absentee ballots. It would provide in this country immeasurable opportunities for a broader classification of people than the very limited numbers of those now eligible to use the proxy, and would be of benefit to those people on vacation or away from their residences for considerable periods of time. It would be a major opening.
However, I am not prepared to take seriously or to agree with the proposition that urban voters, as well as rural voters, should be able to swear in on election day. I have been involved in this business for many years. I have been active in downtown Vancouver and in Vancouver centre, right back to the late forties. I was pretty small then, but not small enough that I could not observe what was going on. From observing downtown Vancouver, Atlantic Canada, southern Ontario and northern Ontario over the years, I came to realize that there are reasons why people can swear in to vote on election day in rural polls where people know each other and are readily identified as being actual residents, and what can happen in a downtown area where no one knows anyone and very seldom knows the person living in the next apartment.
I may be an idealist in some sense, but 1 do not believe in throwing temptation at people and daring them to take up the challenge. There is very often too much at stake in the real business in which we are involved to put that kind of temptation out in front where it counts. There are many reasons for all the rules and regulations, which exist in the elections act which have been built up over the years. The political process is much more alive, democratic and accountable now than it was 20 or 30 years ago, and certainly more than it was 40

June 25, 1981
Canada Elections Act
years ago. It is much more open and honest. While I prefer to think the best of people, I would not want to throw out temptations to encourage them to do their worst.
I said at the beginning that I strongly believe that elections and politicians are too important to be left simply to the politicians. The major reason I oppose the shortening of election campaigns from 60 days down to 47 days, or shortening them by any time when it comes to the number of days from the call of the election to the day on which the ballots are actually cast, is the importance of elections to the people.
I am sure that many hon. members of this House-and certainly those who organize and work for them-realize how vitally important it is that we maximize the number of ordinary people-not the fanatics, not the zealots, and not just the paid hacks-who become involved and feel that they have a vested interest and a real stake in democratic society. For that reason, I do not know nor do I care what my other colleagues, either in this House or in my own party, think about this particular issue. I have been involved in it for much too long in an organizational sense and I have been too involved with digging out ordinary people who are affected by what happens in this place and in other chambers but who, in their day to day life, have other priorities also. It is important to get those people to take some part despite whatever reasons there may be for the shortening of campaigns.
If we limit the period of voluntary involvement, it will give rise to yet another surge of the kind of hyped up media campaigns which I think most members, and I know the Canadian public, find extremely distasteful. It turns them off not only the political process, but it turns many of them off the idea of democratic politicians.
I am opposed to the bill, and that is all I have to say, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) speaking and giving us a point of view which was I suppose, from what one would call a professional from within his party. There are many of us whose experience with elections goes back as far as his but who have gained it on the basis of running in elections themselves. I can assure Your Honour that I weighed what he had to say very carefully, because it seems that while this bill proposes to shorten the time of an election period to 47 days, it also has some very important and complicated consequential amendments. One thing that no one has referred to is the elimination of the different nomination dates, and the elimination of the schedule 3 constituencies. Now everyone is nominated on the same day.
What is the purpose of this bill, besides shortening the period of the election by 12 days? With 282 members in this House, I dare say that there are at least 250 divergent opinions on how the Canada Elections Act could best be devised for a particular individual.
I concede immediately that I, who have a tightly knit urban riding, have nothing in common with a rural riding in the Atlantic provinces, or perhaps one of the less populated constituencies in Newfoundland or, even closer to home, one of the large, entirely rural seats in the prairie provinces. The two constituencies just do not mix. One thing that we have in common is what we feel is the short attention quotient of the average voter. Now that the voter relies more and more on television, we know very well that the attention given to any program depends on the action. As soon as the advertising comes on or as soon as a public affairs program comes on, that is the time to go to the washroom, to put on a pot of coffee or do something else.
The same thing applies to political advertising. There is no point in individual candidates trying to develop a budget which will cover any amount of direct discussion on the issues, on television. The act is stupid in that it has not increased the amount allowed for expenses, yet the cost of printing and television time have escalated far more than the cost of living. Those things are therefore left to the national budgets and that is one of the chief difficulties. In the last election all major parties got their tails caught in a grinder over the nature of their programs. I would be the first to admit that ours was disastrous, as was that of the Liberals. Every time one went out, one had to face irate voters or constituents who had seen the latest episode of nonsensical advertising of the party.
The election campaign nowadays is used by the media to train their young reporters. They go out and listen to a party leader make a speech, then give us their deathless version of what was said, depending upon their own personal prejudice and "the public be damned". That is why there is such a distortion.
While the objective of this bill may be all right, we all suffer from frustration when we consider the inadequacies of the proposed changes. I listened to the intervention of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) on Monday or Tuesday when he said it was quite wrong to talk about matters that were not included in the bill. With the greatest deference to the hon. gentleman, it is at second reading that one speaks about those things which are not in the bill but which should be there to make it effective. As I understand the rules, one cannot speak about new matters on third reading and there is no more resolution stage, so these things have to be debated at second reading. That is the way to conduct a debate in this House. One must be able to talk about those things which are not included.
All I can say is that, regardless of some of the background noise that comes from individuals who stand behind the curtain and refuse to make a speech on the subject, we will carry on. I am glad to see that hon. members have raised particular points which could have been brought forward along with this bill so that they could be considered by committee. When this bill goes to committee, why can it not receive representation on a variety of subjects? Once the bill has been voted upon by the House, the committee will be limited to the consequences of shortening the time from 59 days to 47 days.
June 25, 1981

We could engage in speculation about whether a voter is better apprised of an election, where his polling place will be, what the hours of voting will be, if he gets the little card which is now to be the notice of enumeration, mailed by the deputy returning officer of the constituency, instead of getting a copy of the electoral list of the polls with the information of where the poll will be held and stating that the list is certified, and signed by the deputy returning officer. I do not know that the postmen will be any more faithful in delivering those notices to the enumerators than they were in delivering the voters' lists.
In the past, the voter who was reasonably au fait with what was happening during an election and his right to vote was aware that he was entitled to a copy of the list. He did not have to go down the street about three blocks to see it on a pole. Now there are new aluminum light poles to which a voters' list cannot be attached. In any event, the lists would only last about 24 hours because of the neighbourhood kids delight in tearing them down. It is part of the game. How does "John Q. Citizen" verify that he is on the voters' list? He can go to his party headquarters and ask whether he is on the voters' list. But the individual wonders how dumb people will think he is, not knowing whether he is on the voters' list. Yet he should know he is on the voters' list. That card comes late in the game. It is only determined after the twenty-fifth day before the election. That card will not get to the individual voter because, dear know-it-all parliamentary secretary, on the thirty-fifth day prior to an election, the deputy returning officer starts compiling his lists so they shall be ready no later than the thirtieth day. Then copies are made, some for distribution and some for availability. That is the time during which the list is compiled. Based upon those lists, cards have to be written up, addressed and sent to the individual voter at his or her address. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary can devise something quicker than between the thirtieth and the twenty-fifth day. The twenty-fifth day is the day when the cards are sent out. It is also the time when the deputy returning officer will announce the totals of the preliminary lists upon which the candidate's expense account will be based. Those again are details which come later and later in the game in so far as the candidate is concerned. Incidentally, they apply across the line to all constituencies now, urban and rural. Class three is eliminated. All that will be required now, as I see it, is that nominations are to be held 14 days prior to elections for everyone concerned.
In some parts of the country where I think the greatest pressure comes for shortening the election campaign, nomination day is really when the election campaign starts. That is when the active campaigning takes place in many constituencies in the province of Quebec, constituencies which have been won by both major parties. Very little was done before, except for lining up. There was no door-to-door campaigning. Meetings were held. In these last 14 days, meetings were hot and heavy. People came to hear the issues discussed. But try today to get a meeting together to discuss the issues in any election
Canada Elections Act
outside of sponsored forums. But farming organizations in western Canada, undoubtedly in the province of Ontario and, perhaps across the country, perform a human service in arranging these forums so that candidates from all parties are before the people who want to hear them. That does not help my friend, the hon. member for the Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), however. He has a very difficult time getting around his territory because it is so extensive. Even by chartering aircraft or boats, there is no way that candidates in the western Arctic, the eastern Arctic or in some of the other ridings will see the people in their constituency other than perhaps during a swoop in an aircraft when they can wave and throw out some leaflets. Somebody suggested that he might throw out a few cases of beer too. That is quite wrong, but it has been known to happen. That is another aspect of the campaign.
But we should not pay so much attention to this shortening of time in isolation when there are a lot of changes that could be proposed to help put across a much more intelligent election campaign. For one thing, my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) has a private member's bill in which he proposes that the closing times for the polls be uniform as to the exact moment. In other words, if there are five time zones, there are five different times of closing. We would not have that silly consequence of people in Vancouver, living on Victoria Island or in any part of British Columbia, being four or five hours away from poll closing time, knowing the results from Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces. That is a mockery. This is precisely what we criticize in the U.S. election system, that you can always stampede the last voters by the trends. They like to feel they are part of the bandwagon and if there is a trend toward one party, this will encourage them to do so. That is totally wrong. It is particularly wrong here in Canada. In the last election, for instance, by the time our people were ready to vote two or three hours before poll closing time, and in the city ridings two or three hours before poll closing time is about the time that 70 per cent of the vote is cast, those people knew that what they were doing was not going to help at all. The election was already decided. That is wrong. That amendment, if included in this particular bill, would have been far more meaningful.
There is the question of indexing expenses. Election expenses have now been geared to the 1975 CPI. It has not been changed. It is total nonsense to have that sort of thing.
I find this bill so totally inadequate that I am almost compelled to agree with our colleague from British Columbia that we are not going to have this bill imposed on us piecemeal. This should be part of a meaningful change in the electoral act. There is plenty of time between now and the next election. That is what we should have had in 1979 if the government had thought fit to come forward with this part bill. That would have been fine 18 months ago when elections were imminent. Now it is not so. I would say that it would be far better if we voted against this bill now and told the authors to go back to the drawing boards and come forward with a decent bill.
