speechtext:
Question.

June 25, 1981
Adjournment Debate

A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.
THE ECONOMY-(A) STATEMENTS MADE BY LEADER OF LIBERAL PARTY IN ONTARIO; (B) LOW INTEREST RATE PAID ON GOVERNMENT ANNUITIES

["Order. The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly, this House stands adjourned until tomorrow morning at eleven o'clock.\nAt 10.28 the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.", 'Friday, June 26, 1981']

Mr. Speaker, on Monday, June 22, as recorded in Hansard at page 10838, I put some questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). I used as a basis for my questions statements that had been made over the weekend by the leader of the Liberal party in Ontario to the effect that it was time to impose more taxes on the rich so that the government would have funds to provide more benefits to the poor. Pensioners and others were mentioned in the statement by the Liberal leader in the province of Ontario who had declared inflation to be a Robin Hood in reverse, robbing the poor and benefiting the rich.
Frankly, the purpose of my question was to get to one or two specifics where I felt money should be used for the benefit of those in need. The Minister of Finance said exactly what I thought he would say. He set about telling us that the government has an indexing plan under which all pensioners are thoroughly and completely protected. That is a myth which does not gain any more substance by the telling of it over and over again.
I went from that to one specific group for whom there has been no indexation since 1975. I refer to persons who are holders of Canadian government annuities. For many years the benefits paid under Canadian government annuities were based on interest rates of 3, 7>'h or 4 per cent, sometimes a little more. In 1975 that rate as a basis for a calculation was raised to 7 per cent. There it stands. It is still at 7 per cent.
Accordingly, those who are drawing benefits from Canadian government annuities today are getting pensions which are based on a calculation which assumes that their money is earning interest at the rate of 7 per cent. In fact, interest rates today are twice that or more, and I wanted to ask the minister to do something about it. In view of his claim that the government is prepared to protect pensions, why not do again what was done in 1975, namely, raise the rate of interest used in calculating government annuities?
The Minister of Finance, as he so often does in answering questions, wandered all over the lot and never even mentioned the subject. If one looks at the record in Hansard, he will find at the end I asked, "What about government annuities?" That was my reason for putting the question for a late show. I have already indicated to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) that that would be the thrust of my question. I did not come here tonight to argue about Stuart
Smith. I came here to try to get the answer to the question I was putting to the minister, is it not time to improve payments under Canadian government annuities?
Sometimes when we raise this matter we are told that they are different. Every time something is not done, it is different from the area where something is being done. We are told that this is a contract and that that contract cannot be upset. Canada Pension Plan benefits are a contract. Old age security is a contract, for if you live in this country and pay taxes, you get old age security. Pensions under various superannuation plans are all contracts, so there is no weight to that argument at all. Canada Savings Bonds are certainly contracts. They are bought at a certain rate of interest that is printed right there in the bond. Yet the government has now come to the realization that with inflation the way it is, it has to adjust these interest rates. Why are the holders of Canadian government annuities left out in the cold? I know that in 1975 we were told, "do not look for this every year, it is not permanent, it is just a one-shot effort." But the facts of the matter are that inflation has got much worse, and this is one group the government seems to have forgotten. I would like to hear from the parliamentary secretary tonight, now that he knows this is the thrust of my question, whether the government is giving consideration to doing now in 1981, or certainly not later than 1982, what was done in 1975, namely to increase the benefits under the Canadian Government Annuities Act. I confess that I have a personal interest in that piece of legislation. As I have said a good many times, it was passed the day I was born. I do not like to see it stifled.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg Centre (Mr. Knowles) is essentially seeking, as we have all heard, an increase in the rate of interest paid on Government of Canada annuities. As the hon. member indicated, they are, indeed, long-term assets if the legislation was introduced on the day he was born.
Seventy-three years ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Members will recall that the act provided, as the hon. member mentioned, for a change in those rates effective April 1, 1975. At that time annuities that were paying between 3 per cent and 514 per cent were raised to the level of 7 per cent.
Undoubtedly the hon. member is aware of Section 5(2) of the Government Annuities Improvement Act which reads:
The governor in council may, by regulation, amend the schedule in respect of any annuities or category of annuities.
Pursuant to this provision, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has been closely monitoring the appropriateness of the rate of interest payable on government annuities. In assessing whether this rate of interest should be increased, it is important to bear in mind a number of considerations which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has brought to our attention. Foremost
June 25, 1981

perhaps, is the contractual nature of annuities and the potential effects of a substantial change to the terms of these contracts on other financial instruments, both in the public and the private sector. Related to this is the fundamental issue of the equity of an increase in this rate vis-a-vis all those other Canadians who are also adversely affected by inflation and high interest rates, such as investors in other Government of Canada long-term instruments.
The government's present assessment of the situation, which includes a comparison with returns earned on similar instruments in the private sector as well as an appreciation of the over-all implications of a further positive adjustment, is that no such adjustment should be made at this time. In this connection, it is important to bear in mind that comparisons with rates of interest payable on short-term financial instruments, such as Canada Savings Bonds and guaranteed investment certificates, are misleading in that they overlook the fundamentally different nature of these instruments we are referring to here. This is particularly inappropriate in a situation characterized by high and volatile, short-term interest rates such as we now have.
The government continues to be of the view that the only viable solution to this difficult problem lies in the pursuit of monetary and fiscal policies which will serve to reduce inflation and thereby reduce interest rates for all Canadians. To the extent that narrowly targeted measures of relief lead to pressures for more broader-based measures, these are difficult to reconcile with the ultimate objective of the government.

The government is wrong again.
ENERGY-(A) REQUEST FOR REDUCTION IN FEDERAL SHARE OF REVENUES; (B) ENERGY TAX REBATE PROGRAM

Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of last year the price of gasoline at the gas pump in Ontario has increased by 60 cents per gallon. There have been 12 increases in the price of oil products since March, 1980, and all but three of these were increases in federal taxes; not an increase to producers, to refiners or dealers, but an increase to the federal Liberal government. The federal share of the increase in the price of gasoline at the pump is 36 cents per gallon, a 36-cent per gallon increase in federal taxes alone. That is twice as high as the 18-cent per gallon increase proposed by my party, the Progressive Conservative party, just over one year ago.
Our proposal of 18 cents would not only have gone toward the subsidization of offshore imports, it would have provided an energy tax rebate to low and middle-income families, an energy tax rebate for farmers, an energy tax rebate for fishermen and an energy tax rebate for urban transit. In other words, our national energy policy would have led Canada toward energy self-sufficiency during the next decade while at the same time protecting those who could afford increases the least. We had a pricing agreement with the producing provinces in principle, and the only agreement the Liberals have today is an agreement to purchase more oil from offshore. We
Adjournment Debate
have more dependence on offshore imports, and we all know the price differential. The cost of a barrel of oil from offshore averages $43. In Canada, the cost is $17.75 per barrel. But the Liberals prefer to pay higher prices for offshore oil and to ask all Canadians to subsidize the difference. The subsidization has reached staggering $5,158 billion this year alone. We pay for it, and that subsidization is growing.
What did the Liberals say before those increases took place? In the 1980 election campaign, for example, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) went from one side of the country to the other saying, "Vote Liberal, and energy prices will stay down". That is what the minister said last February. However, we do not have to go that far back. On May 27, 1980, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) said: "Every rise of one dollar a barrel in oil and its equivalent in gas increases the rate of inflation by almost half a percentage point". I agree with that. We all agree with that, but the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his government have increased the price of gasoline at the gas pump and the price of energy generally in Canada. It has not been to the producers or refiners, at least not to the tune of 36 cents per gallon. That is the information provided to us by the minister's department. It is no wonder we now have a record high inflation rate which leads to record high interest rates which lead to a record high cost of living and which leads back to record high inflation.
Then, believe it or not, the travelling Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-who is too busy to answer questions in the House because he is meeting with his new socialist friend, the President of France-said in this House on June 9, 1981, when speaking about energy revenues: "We would like the over-all result to be the federal government's sharing 23 per cent or 25 per cent of the take". That is my whole point. The Prime Minister would be satisfied if the federal government took in 23 per cent or 25 per cent of the take of energy revenues.
The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has provided us with the following information. In Ontario-and we must look at this one province at a time because prices differ in various provinces due to provincial taxes and other matters-the price of gasoline at the pump is $1.66. The federal take through such charges as sales taxes, excise taxes and the Canadian ownership charge so that Petro-Canada could nationalize Petrofina, is 56 cents, or 33.7 per cent. If the Prime Minister would stay in this country long enough I would like to ask him, if he would be satisfied with a 23 per cent or 25 per cent take of energy prices, why the government does not now lower energy taxes across the board to at least 25 per cent. If the government is not willing to do that, it should at least be compassionate enough to bring in an energy tax rebate to be taken from the excessive revenues it gets from energy resources. The government should be compassionate enough to bring in energy tax rebates along the lines of those the Progressive Conservative party proposed in the Crosbie budget.

June 25, 1981
Adjournment Debate

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: God help us.

Yes, energy tax rebates-I hear guffaws across the way-for low and middle-income families. The Liberals said: "Let us not increase the price by 18 cents." They have more than doubled the taxes. There is no energy tax rebate for low and middle-income families. Why no energy tax rebate for fishermen, farmers and urban transit? Those are the questions we and Canadians are asking, and those are the questions I want answered today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member opposite is in such a state of confusion and so befuddled by his pseudo statistics that he clearly has no real understanding of the situation with regard to oil pricing in Canada today. The fact is that at the Toronto pump the price of a litre of gasoline is less today than it would have been under the Conservative formula.
Let us examine the situation in its true light. The fact is the recent increases are composed of a number of factors. For example, wellhead price increases under the Liberals between January 1, 1980 and January 1, 1981, amounted to $4. Under the Conservative budget, it would have amounted to $6.25.
Hogwash.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The Syncrude levy, an important part of the total cost at the pump, was and would have been pursued by the Conservative government had it been able to hold on to office. That increase would have been automatic whatever government was in office. Also, the petroleum compensation charge to offset the higher cost of imported oil would, in the Conservative case, have had to be found from general revenues. It is imposed at the pump itself in our case. I do not think there can be any doubt which is the preferable way of imposing that levy. The compensation charge, that money does not go into the general revenues of the government; it is passed on to the refiners. For the hon. member to speak as if somehow that charge was to the benefit of government revenue is to simply misunderstand the situation in Canada today.
As for the special compensation charge to offset the cost of additional imported oil in light of the production cutbacks by government of Alberta, we have indicated that if Alberta restores production, that levy would be immediately removed.
Finally, the Canadian ownership charge brings real benefit to all Canadians through acquisition of assets for the national oil company, Petro-Canada; in this particular case the acquisition of Petrofina. So not only are prices lower in Toronto today than they would have been under the Conservative government, but the other benefits of the Liberal policy should now be evident to the hon. member opposite who is in such a state of confusion about the true state of affairs.
How can you say that with a straight face.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Simmons (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-RESULT OF MINISTER'S DISCUSSIONS ON ACID RAIN WITH UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF THE INTERIOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all let me thank my colleague and friend, the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), for raising this issue in the adjournment debate tonight. It is an issue which is coming in for a lot of discussion, and so it should. We welcome the opportunity to discuss it here again this evening.
I believe his concern is well founded. I hope I am wrong. For that reason, I hope he is wrong. However, we get some disconcerting signs from the United States. We saw the leaked cabinet document, in the last week or so on the subject of proposed revisions of the Clean Air Act in the U.S. We saw some of the appointments to positions of environmental authority in the United States. Frankly, they constitute fairly disconcerting signals.
Against that, we have a number of assurances which have been given to us by the U.S. administration, both by the former administration of Mr. Carter and by the present administration of Mr. Reagan, and assurances from the office of President, right on down to other positions of authority in this particular area.
First of all, let me just reflect for a moment on the memorandum of intent which was signed last August between the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) for Canada and the then secretary of state of the U.S., Mr. Muskie. First, that memorandum committed both countries to begin formal negotiations by June of this year, which is this very month.
Adjournment Debate
Second, it also provided for five joint working groups to do some work preparatory to the beginning of negotiations. Third, it committed both countries to taking certain interim control measures under existing legal authorities to reduce transboundary air pollution.
As I say, that memorandum was signed last August under the former administration of Mr. Carter. As Your Honour will know, Mr. Reagan was here in Ottawa some months ago in March. At that time, in meetings with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and with the Minister of the Environment, the U.S. President gave full commitment that the undertaking and the memorandum of intent of last August would be honoured, that it was the U.S. administration's intent to pursue the work of the five working groups that I mentioned earlier, and it was also its intent to begin negotiations with Canada in the month of June of this year.
Subsequent to that particular meeting, the Minister of the Environment went to Washington and met with the new secretary of the interior, Mr. Watt. At that time, we received similar assurances to that which we had received from the U.S. President earlier.
Two days ago, the negotiations actually began in Washington. They were somewhat clouded by the uncertainties over the Clean Air Act review in the United States. On that particular subject, the Canadian delegation recorded very strong concern that domestic regulation be adequate to deal effectively with transboundary air pollution.
Finally, let me say that as we see it, the battle is far from over. We in Canada cannot let up for a minute. There are strong lobbies in Washington which want to convince the U.S. administration that there is no problem. There is a lack of awareness among the American public. Our job is twofold. First, we want to raise that awareness. We are doing that through pamphlets which we are distributing in the U.S., through speech-making in the U.S., and we are also continuing to impress upon the U.S. administration the need to honour its commitment made last August, and subsequently.
